https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Michigan High School Athletic Association Representative Council meeting held in East Lansing on May 3, 2021, distributed to member districts with the instruction that changes take effect Aug. 1, 2021 unless otherwise indicated. The Council adopted rule changes across regulations, officiating, and individual sports, including a move of all fall high school practice starts to Monday, Aug. 9, 2021, permanent authorization of multi-school district cooperative programs in nine sports, adoption of girls wrestling as an individual division, and a CPR certification attestation for head coaches. It also approved the 2021-22 budget, which forecasts an addition in cash of $818,301.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Meeting**
MHSAA Representative Council, East Lansing, May 3, 2021. Mark Uyl served as recorder. Eighteen Council members were present (including Eric Albright of Midland, Nicole Carter of Novi, Karen Leinaar of Bear Lake, Vic Michaels of Detroit, and Alex Tiseo of Marquette); Jay Alexander of Detroit was absent. Scott Eldridge and Bill Zaagman of Lansing also attended. Minutes of the March 26, 2021 Council meeting and the March 25 and April 21, 2021 Executive Committee meetings were approved on a motion by Kris Isom, supported by Chris Miller.

**Administration report**

| Measure | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| High school members, 2020-21 (as of April 1, 2021) | 747 |
| Junior high/middle school members (as of April 1, 2021) | 751 |
| Comparable figures as of April 1, 2019 | 753 and 819 |
| Elementary schools with 6th-grade participation | 69 |
| High school cooperative agreements / teams (as of April 4, 2019) | 355 / 640 |
| Junior high-middle school cooperative agreements / teams | 86 / 330 |
| Eligibility advancement applications, 2020-21 | 0 (lowest since 1987-88; high was 94 in 1991-92) |
| Educational Transfer Forms, 2020-21 through April 5, 2021 | 110 (213 in 2019-20; 266 in 2015-16) |
| Out-of-State Practice travel forms, 2020-21 | 6 (72 prior year) |
| Athletic Director In-Service/Update registrants | more than 732 |
| Coaches Advancement Program participants, 2021-22 | more than 2,000, with over 1,200 in CAP 1 |

Public-to-public transfers were the most common category (67) and the divorce exception (#8) the most frequent reason (40). More than 33,000 CAP levels will have been completed since the start of 2004-05. Officials' registrations continued a decade-long decline.

**Ongoing business**
A task force was formed to meet three times over spring and summer on out-of-season contact days. The waiver of the previous academic record regulation (Regulation I, Section 7) was extended for fall 2021 sports. All fall high school practices move to Monday, Aug. 9, 2021, and thereafter to the 16th Monday before Thanksgiving. Multi-school district cooperative programs in baseball, bowling, girls competitive cheer, cross country, golf, soccer, girls softball, tennis, and wrestling were made permanent notwithstanding the 3,500-student enrollment maximum.

**Regulations**
The Council voted not to print the 2021-22 Handbook, providing a password-protected online version instead. It amended Regulation I, Section 4, Interpretation 24 on 8th/9th grade classwork; Regulation I, Section 12(C) on all-star events, requiring written notice at least 30 calendar days prior; and Regulation II, Section 3(B) requiring CPR certification attestation for head coaches, with the non-varsity requirement effective Aug. 1, 2022.

**Sports and officials actions**
Adopted: Phantom bowling oil pattern; competitive cheer choreography study and two technical changes; sideline officials switching sides at halftime; iWanamaker golf scoring; a black quarter-zip option for gymnastics officials; a softball suspended-game policy mirroring baseball's 2020 policy; a 117-game daily tennis limit and revised seed-withdrawal handling; girls wrestling as an individual division (D1, D2, D3, D4, Girls); and a late arrival skin check. Not approved: expansion of the football 5-quarter rule, playoff region seeding by playoff points, and a tennis opt-up letter requirement. The officials rating system replaces the 1-5 scale with four categories, and baseball Quarterfinal assignments move to four umpires, increasing umpires selected at that level by 16.

**Budget and future meetings**
Two budget deficits in excess of $670,000 occurred in two of the past four years. The 2021-22 budget forecasts an addition in cash of $818,301 and a profit of $318,301 after repayment of the line-of-credit loan; salaries remain frozen. Next meetings: Dec. 3, 2021; Friday, March 25, 2022; and May 1-2, 2022, the latter to be held at Treetops Resort in Gaylord.

Accounts of Meetings. Motion by Kris Isom, supported by Chris Miller, to approve the minutes of the Representative Council meeting of March 26, 2021, and the Executive Committee meeting minutes of March 25 and April 21, 2021. Adopted.

Administration report. MHSAA membership during 2020-21 was 747 high schools and 751 junior high/middle schools as of April 1, 2021, compared with 753 and 819 respectively as of April 1, 2019. There were also 69 elementary schools with 6th-grader participation. As of April 4, 2019 there were 355 cooperative program agreements for high schools covering 640 teams, an increase of 16 programs and 33 teams over the previous year, and 86 cooperative program agreements covering 330 teams for junior high/middle schools, an increase of 1 program and 5 teams. The most frequent high school cooperative sports, in order, are ice hockey, boys and girls swimming and diving, girls softball, and boys lacrosse; at the junior high/middle school level they are boys and girls track and field, boys and girls cross country, and wrestling. No eligibility advancement applications were received during 2020-21, the lowest number since the provision began in 1987-88, compared with 3 during 2019-20, 3 during 2018-19, 6 during 2017-18, 5 during 2016-17, 5 during 2015-16, 4 during 2014-15, 14 during 2013-14, 15 during 2012-13, 9 during 2011-12, 15 during 2010-11, 2009-10 and 2008-09, and 7 during 2007-08; the highest was 94 during 1991-92. There were 110 Educational Transfer Forms processed for 2020-21 through April 5, 2021, a figure the report says cannot be compared to prior years because of the pandemic and because all spring sports transfers were eligible in 2020-21; prior-year counts were 213 for 2019-20, 215 for 2018-19, 219 for 2017-18, 237 for 2016-17, and 266 for 2015-16. Public-to-public school transfers remain the most common at 67, and the divorce exception (#8) remains the most frequent reason at 40. Six Travel Forms for Out-of-State Practice were filed during 2020-21 compared to 72 the year before; the highest number filed was 113 during 2007-08 and the lowest 40 during 2003-04, with the requirement beginning in 1994-95. A listing of violations by schools and officials between April 9, 2020 and April 8, 2021 showed a total much lower than previous years because of cancelled contests and seasons. Virtual Athletic Director In-Service and Update Meeting programs attracted more than 732 registrants in 2020-21; for the 11th year, two in-service programs for athletic department administrative assistants are planned for September. The Coaches Advancement Program has already involved more than 2,000 participants in 2021-22 with over 1,200 registrations in CAP 1, and by the end of the year individuals will have completed more than 33,000 CAP levels since the start of 2004-05. The decade-long decline in officials' registrations continued through 2020-21, with the pandemic complicating recruiting and retention. Officials Reports for spring 2020, fall 2020, and winter 2020-21 were provided, broken down by sport and by level (varsity, junior varsity, and sometimes 9th, 8th, and 7th grade); sportsmanship problems were described as statistically rare. From the National Federation of State High School Associations, the Reaching Higher event in girls volleyball will not be held in summer 2021, with final decisions on basketball summer plans due by May 15.

Legislation and litigation. Bill Zaagman reported that the State Legislature's current focus is the budget process and that he will continue monitoring bills affecting the association. Scott Eldridge reported the MHSAA is not involved in public, legislative, or judicial challenges, and provided an update on recent COVID-19 legal activity involving MDHHS and local health departments.

Ongoing business. On the COVID-19 update, the Council discussed the financial impact of the pandemic and the formation of a task force to meet three times during spring and summer to discuss out-of-season contact days and develop concrete proposals for school discussion and input during fall 2021. Staff will send a summer guidance document reminding schools that the traditional summer dead period regulation remains in place. Motion by Vic Michaels, supported by John Thompson, to extend the waiver of the previous academic record regulation (Regulation I, Section 7) for sports played in fall 2021. Adopted. On the common fall practice date, motion by Chris Miller, supported by Eric Albright, to move the start of all fall high school sports practices to Monday, Aug. 9, 2021; beginning in fall 2021 all high school fall sports may begin practice on the 16th Monday before Thanksgiving, the same as football. Adopted. Staff provided a volleyball scheduling update on input from administrators and coaches regarding the MHSAA Finals and the length of the season, noting the issue also involves the start date of winter sports. On multi-school district cooperative programs, the Council recalled that in May 2016 it approved a two-year experiment, extended for two additional school years through 2020-21, allowing two or more schools of the same public school district with the same governing board to apply for cooperative programs in nine sports regardless of the 3,500-student enrollment maximum: baseball, bowling, girls competitive cheer, cross country, golf, soccer, girls softball, tennis, and wrestling, subject to a demonstrated history of inadequate participant numbers and not approvable on financial grounds. Motion by Vic Michaels, supported by Karen Leinaar, to approve these programs on a permanent basis with the same requirements as all other programs, including the two-year renewal process with league approval. Adopted. Fall Tour planning anticipates a normal Update tour with remote alternatives, covering lessons of the pandemic in remote learning and instruction, potential use of school transportation in the summer, classification and cooperative program limits, out-of-season regulations, basketball contest limitations, and the length of the girls volleyball and basketball seasons.

Regulations. Regulations I through V of the MHSAA Handbook and their interpretations were submitted for review. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Jason Mensing, to not print the MHSAA Handbook for the 2021-22 school year only and to provide an online password-protected version for administrators, with a printed and emailed supplement of changes and calendars for 2021-22 and beyond also placed online and provided to schools. Adopted. Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Steve Newkirk, to approve the consent package of miscellaneous changes for organization, clarity, or updating and to incorporate previously adopted changes or interpretations. Adopted. Regulation I, Section 4, Interpretation 24: motion by John Thompson, supported by Jason Mensing, addressing students whose classwork is divided between the 8th and 9th grades, who are considered enrolled in the grade where they take the major part of their work in that term, with ties resolved to the 8th grade; a student who has completed the 7th grade at any school may be considered an 8th grader if the student does not exceed the enrollment threshold of Interpretation 46, namely enrollment in 3 high school classes of 4 taken in the 8th grade, 4 or 5 of 6, 5 of 7, or 6 of 8; this 66% allowance applies only to a student enrolled for the first time in the 8th grade and not to a student repeating the 8th grade, and a student not in the 9th grade or higher is ineligible for senior high athletics except as provided in Regulation I, Section 1(D) and Regulation III, Section 2(B). Adopted. Regulation I, Section 12(C): motion by Chris Riker, supported by Chris Miller, allowing a student who has completed a 12th-grade season in a sport to participate without loss of eligibility for other sports in one high school all-star event in that sport held after the MHSAA Final, provided the student is eligible under all MHSAA regulations including academic eligibility and amateur status, the event requires or receives no financial support from an MHSAA member school or school-related organization, and participation is approved by the principal or athletic director with written notice to the MHSAA at least 30 calendar days prior to the event. Adopted. Regulation II, Section 3(B): motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Kris Isom, requiring high schools to attest by each season's established deadline that all head coaches of each high school team (varsity, JV, or 9th grade) hold valid current CPR certification, with the requirement for non-varsity head coaches taking effect Aug. 1, 2022; the deadline is the latest date set for completion of the MHSAA rules meeting for the sport, a person who is head coach for more than one sport must meet the deadline for the first, and schools are expected to impose the penalty of Section 8(B) on varsity head coaches who do not comply, extended effective Aug. 1, 2022 to JV and 9th-grade coaches. Adopted. The Council also discussed extending the requirement to middle schools and was updated on a fall discussion item allowing school transportation for out-of-season summer activities.

Classification, athletic equity, and officials. The Summary of MHSAA Tournament Classification for 2021-22 was provided, with future committee topics to include a possible fifth division in sports where 600 or more schools sponsor the sport. Motion by Chris Miller, supported by Chris Riker, to approve the Athletic Equity Committee recommendation to publish a statement encouraging local review of nicknames and logos considered offensive or hurtful to minority groups, stating that the MHSAA recognizes the importance of equity in high school sports, that schools and mascots are rich in tradition and unique to each community, and that the MHSAA encourages member schools and communities to evaluate and reconsider names and mascots that may be offensive. Adopted; schools will be encouraged to review the information at fall Update and Athletic Director In-Service sessions, and the Council discussed a possible sanction of barring such schools from hosting tournaments. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Jason Mensing, to adjust the officials rating system for 2021-22 to encourage more ratings from schools with a simpler format, eliminating the 1-5 rating in favor of four categories: judgement, presence and demeanor, attitude and effort, and administration and communication. Adopted. Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Chris Miller, to change baseball umpire assignments at the Quarterfinal round from three umpires officiating three games with two umpires each to four umpires officiating the two Regional Final games with two umpires and the Quarterfinal game with all four, increasing the number of umpires selected at this level by 16 and matching softball practice. Adopted.

Sports Medicine and committees. The Sports Medicine Advisory Committee reported ongoing discussion of providing the Pre-participation Physical Exam on a two-year cycle with an interim Health Questionnaire in intervening years, noting that health history is the most important part of the exam and that the Health Questionnaire was established with good results in 2020-21. Council members were supplied with committee descriptions, appointment procedures, candidate lists, and a list of schools unrepresented for five years, and were encouraged to nominate superintendents, principals, small schools, females, minorities, and unrepresented schools. Committee members for 2021-22 will be published in benchmarks, and staff suggested all committee meetings remain virtual for 2021-22.

Sports activities. Bowling: motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Don Gustafson, to adopt the Phantom oil pattern for the 2021-22 bowling season. Adopted. Girls competitive cheer: motion by Kris Isom, supported by Vic Michaels, to continue studying a new choreography chart awarding points based on team tumble, OLEs, vertical twist/360s, and release skills. Adopted. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Nicole Carter, to allow a connected tumbling skill to count as a new variety point for Round 3 and to allow four difficulty points for a one-leg flair at the elevator level for middle schools. Adopted. Football: motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Eric Albright, to not approve expanding the 5-quarter rule to exempt special teams play. Adopted (no change). Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Kris Isom, requiring sideline officials (linesman and line judge) to change sidelines at halftime for all varsity contests, optional at subvarsity. Adopted. Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Chris Miller, to not approve seeding Playoff Regions based on playoff points. Adopted (no change). Golf: motion by John Thompson, supported by Karen Leinaar, requiring use of the iWanamaker scoring program and app during the regular season beginning in 2021-22. Adopted. Girls gymnastics: motion by John Thompson, supported by Karen Leinaar, adding an option for officials to wear a specified black quarter-zip with the MHSAA logo. Adopted. Boys lacrosse: a committee recommendation on voluntary coach/player contact days was referred to the task force created under the COVID-19 update for review prior to August 2021. Softball: motion by Don Gustafson, supported by John Thompson, adding a suspended game policy under which a game is suspended if called before reaching regulation or if called with the score tied, mirroring the baseball policy approved in 2020. Adopted. Tennis: motion by Vic Michaels, supported by Kris Isom, limiting a player to no more than 117 games in a given day. Adopted. Motion by Chris Riker, supported by Don Gustafson, on adjusting seeds when a seeded player withdraws on the day of the tournament. Adopted. Motion by John Thompson, supported by Karen Leinaar, to not approve requiring a letter when a school opts up in tennis. Adopted (no change). Wrestling: motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Kris Isom, adding girls wrestling as an individual division rather than a new sport (D1, D2, D3, D4, Girls) using a sectionals concept with a qualifying event before the Finals, with girls still allowed to wrestle on boys teams during the team postseason. Adopted. Motion by John Thompson, supported by Don Gustafson, approving a late arrival skin check for multiple dual meets in the regular season. Adopted.

Operations. Motion by Chris Miller, supported by Jason Mensing, to approve the Quick Reference Calendars for 2021-22 and 2022-23 and the seven-year calendar of MHSAA events. Adopted. Council members were invited to vote for up to two Allen W. Bush Award candidates from the five presented, with winners notified in May, honored during fall 2021 or early 2022, and featured in the fall issue of benchmarks. The next Representative Council meeting is Dec. 3, 2021 at the MHSAA office in East Lansing; the March meeting will be the morning of Friday, March 25, 2022 in East Lansing; and the May meeting will be Sunday and Monday, May 1 and 2, 2022. Motion by Sean Jacques, supported by Karen Leinaar, to hold the May 2022 meeting at Treetops Resort in Gaylord. Adopted.

Budget. The report states that since COVID hit in March 2020 the association has managed unprecedented times with severe reductions in tournament revenue, aided by the sacrifices of member schools and tournament hosts in 2020-21. While two installments of the federal Payroll Protection program have been helpful, the reality of two budget deficits in excess of $670,000 in two of the past four years still exists. The 2021-22 budget proposes a modest increase in most ticket prices beyond the entry level of the tournament, allowing prompt repayment of a line-of-credit loan and rebuilding of reserves. The MHSAA anticipates a break-even 2020-21 fiscal year with an average spring tournament season. Staff salaries will remain frozen for 2021-22, including the hiring of three new staff members following the retirements of Nate Hampton and Peggy Montpas and the departure of Faye Verellen. The 2021-22 budget forecasts an addition in cash of $818,301 and a profit of $318,301 after repayment of the line-of-credit loan from last spring and fall. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Kris Isom, to approve the 2021-22 budget. Adopted.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Summary of the Michigan High School Athletic Association's Athletes and Officials Accident Medical and Concussion Care insurance programs distributed to high schools and junior high/middle schools for 2020-21. The accident medical policy, provided at no cost since the 1970-71 school year, pays up to $1,000,000 in medical expenses per claim after a $25,000 deductible in paid medical expenses has been met. A separate concussion care program in place since 2015-16 carries a policy limit of $25,000 for each accident and reimburses deductibles and co-pays left unpaid by other coverage.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Program overview**
Since the 1970-71 school year the MHSAA has provided participants at each member school and all registered officials with insurance intended to help pay excess accident medical bills for injuries sustained in athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction. The MHSAA is the policyholder and pays the premium; coverage is provided at no cost to eligible athletes of member schools and to registered officials. The document states it is not intended to be a complete description of coverage and exclusions.

**Who and what is covered**
Coverage applies to grades 6-12 for students accidentally injured while engaged in interscholastic athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction, namely baseball, basketball (boys and girls), bowling (boys and girls), cross country (boys and girls), football, golf (boys and girls), gymnastics (girls), competitive cheer (girls), ice hockey, lacrosse (boys and girls), soccer (boys and girls), softball (girls), alpine skiing (boys and girls), swimming and diving (boys and girls), tennis (boys and girls), track and field (boys and girls), volleyball (girls), and wrestling. Students are covered in sports ending with an MHSAA tournament provided their principal attests in writing and the MHSAA agrees they were eligible under all MHSAA regulations at the time of injury. Coverage extends to travel directly to and from a scheduled event in school-sponsored transportation and to in-season participation in an allowed activity under the direct supervision of a full-time school employee or designated coach.

**Exclusions and edge cases**
Student-athletes ineligible under MHSAA regulations are not covered. Students ineligible under local school rules but eligible under MHSAA rules are covered if allowed to practice with the team, as are students suspended from contests under Regulation V, Section 3 who continue practicing. Officials must be on the premises of the contest worked. Sideline cheerleaders are covered while traveling in school-sponsored transportation and while cheering under supervision of a designated school employee, provided their activity does not exceed the safety norms of MHSAA Girls Competitive Cheer. The insurance does not cover any out-of-season activities or activities occurring beyond the mileage limits of Regulation II, Section 6, Interpretation 193, even if not expressly prohibited.

**Accident medical benefits**

| Benefit | Amount / condition |
| --- | --- |
| Medical expense limit | up to $1,000,000 per claim |
| Deductible | $25,000 in paid medical expenses per claim |
| Paralysis or coma cash benefit | up to $50,000, if occurring within 180 days after the accident |
| Certification waiting period | physician certifies permanence after a 16-month waiting period |
| First medical expense | must be incurred within 90 days after the accident |
| Accidental death or dismemberment | $10,000 if the event occurs within 365 days |

The MHSAA-arranged program pays medical expenses above the $25,000 deductible left unpaid by parents' or officials' insurance or other sources such as school-purchased insurance.

**Concussion care insurance**
Provided since the 2015-16 school year to athletic participants at each MHSAA member junior high/middle school and high school, paying accident medical expense benefits resulting from concussion sustained while participating in an MHSAA in-season covered activity (in-season practice or competition). Policy limit is $25,000 for each accident, with covered students, sports, and situations following the accident medical insurance. The program is intended to assure that all eligible student-athletes in grades 6 through 12, male and female, in all levels of all sports under MHSAA jurisdiction receive prompt professional attention for head injury events even if uninsured or under-insured.

**Claims administrators**
Accident medical: Mr. Bryan Cronen, FIRST AGENCY, INC., 5071 West H Avenue, Kalamazoo, MI 49009-8501, phone 269.381.6630, fax 269.381.3055, bcronen@1stagency.com. Concussion care: Ms. Terri Bruner, K & K Insurance Group, 1712 Magnavox Way, Fort Wayne, IN 46801, phone 800-237-2917, fax 312-381-9077, Terri.Bruner@kandkinsurance.com. Districts are advised to make sure all high schools and junior high/middle schools are designated by their board of education as MHSAA member schools so athletes at both levels are covered by the MHSAA-purchased plan.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Informational summary titled "Athletes and Officials Accident Medical & Concussion Insurance," issued by the Michigan High School Athletic Association to high schools and junior high/middle schools for the 2020-21 school year. The document carries the caveat that it is not intended to be a complete description of coverage and exclusions.

History and purpose. Since the 1970-71 school year the MHSAA has provided participants at each member school and all registered officials with insurance intended to help pay excess accident medical bills to administer to injuries sustained in athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction. The MHSAA is the policyholder and pays the premium for this layer of accident medical coverage, and the coverage is provided at no cost to the eligible athletes of MHSAA member schools and to registered officials.

Scope of covered activity. Coverage is provided for grades 6-12 for all students accidentally injured while engaged in interscholastic athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction. The enumerated sports are baseball; basketball (boys and girls); bowling (boys and girls); cross country (boys and girls); football; golf (boys and girls); gymnastics (girls); competitive cheer (girls); ice hockey; lacrosse (boys and girls); soccer (boys and girls); softball (girls); alpine skiing (boys and girls); swimming and diving (boys and girls); tennis (boys and girls); track and field (boys and girls); volleyball (girls); and wrestling.

Eligibility conditions. All eligible students who participate in interscholastic athletic activities at an MHSAA member school in sports which end with an MHSAA tournament are covered provided their school principal attests in writing and the MHSAA agrees that they were eligible under all MHSAA regulations at the time of the injury. Eligible student athletes are covered while traveling directly to and from a scheduled event as a representative of the school in transportation sponsored by the school, and while participating in season in an allowed activity under the direct supervision of a full-time school employee or a coach designated by the school acting within the scope of his or her coaching duties, in those sports for which the MHSAA provides a tournament series.

Ineligibility and special cases. Student-athletes ineligible under MHSAA regulations are not covered. Students who are ineligible under local school rules but would be eligible under MHSAA rules are covered if they were allowed to practice with their school team. Students who are otherwise eligible but suspended from contests under Regulation V, Section 3 (contest disqualifications) are covered if they continue practicing with the school team. Officials must be on the premises of the contest worked to be covered under the policy. Sideline cheerleaders are covered while traveling directly to and from interscholastic athletic events as a representative of the school in school-sponsored transportation, and while cheering at interscholastic athletic events under the direct supervision of a school employee designated by the school; to be covered by MHSAA-purchased insurance, the activity of sideline cheerleaders at interscholastic athletic events must not exceed the safety norms of MHSAA Girls Competitive Cheer, meaning the height of mounts, flips, stunts, and similar elements. The document states in emphasized text that MHSAA Accident Medical Insurance does not cover any out-of-season activities or any activities occurring beyond the mileage limits of Regulation II, Section 6, Interpretation 193, even if those activities are not expressly prohibited by the MHSAA.

Accident medical benefit structure. The policy will pay up to $1,000,000 in medical expenses after a deductible of $25,000 in paid medical expenses per claim has been met. The MHSAA-arranged program then pays medical expenses above the $25,000 deductible left unpaid by the parents' or official's insurance or any other sources such as school-purchased insurance. A cash benefit payment of up to $50,000 will be made if a covered person is paralyzed or in a coma within 180 days after the accident; payment will not be made until a physician certifies that, after a 16-month waiting period, the injury is permanent and irreversible, and this payment must result in disability and is in addition to payments already covered for medical expenses. The first medical expense must be incurred within 90 days after the date of the accident. An accidental death or dismemberment benefit of $10,000 is paid if either event occurs within 365 days of the date.

Accident medical claims administration. The claims administrator is Mr. Bryan Cronen, FIRST AGENCY, INC., 5071 West H Avenue, Kalamazoo, MI 49009-8501, phone 269.381.6630, fax 269.381.3055, email bcronen@1stagency.com.

District action item. The document instructs in emphasized text that districts make sure all high schools and junior high/middle schools in the district are designated by their board of education as MHSAA member schools so athletes on both levels are covered by the MHSAA-purchased plan.

Concussion care insurance. Since the 2015-16 school year the MHSAA has provided athletic participants at each MHSAA member junior high/middle school and high school with insurance intended to pay accident medical expense benefits resulting from concussion. The suspected concussion must be sustained while the athlete is participating in an MHSAA in-season covered activity, defined as in-season practice or competition. The policy limit is $25,000 for each accident. Covered students, sports, and situations follow those of the accident medical insurance described above. The program intends to assure that all eligible student-athletes in MHSAA member schools in grades 6 through 12, male and female, in all levels of all sports under MHSAA jurisdiction receive prompt and professional attention for head injury events even if the child is uninsured or under-insured, and accident medical deductibles and co-pays left unpaid by other policies are reimbursed under this program.

Concussion claims administration. The claims administrator is Ms. Terri Bruner, K & K Insurance Group, 1712 Magnavox Way, Fort Wayne, IN 46801, phone 800-237-2917, fax 312-381-9077, email Terri.Bruner@kandkinsurance.com.

The administration recommends using Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projections as the basis for admissions and accepting Schools of Choice applications for 50 Kindergarten, 50 First Grade and 20 Middle School students, admitting 50 kindergarteners initially with the option to admit more in the third week of August if space allows. **Purpose and authorship**
A presentation plus memorandum on Schools of Choice (SOC) for the 2021-2022 school year, authored by Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, and Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction. **Sibling preference survey**

**Recommendations**
Use Plante Moran Cresa projections as the foundation for setting SOC admissions; accept applications for 50 Kindergarten, 50 First Grade and 20 Middle School students; admit 50 kindergarteners initially with the option to admit additional students in the third week of August if space allows; place middle school students in buildings according to available space. Factors considered were current district enrollment, enrollment projections and trends, current SOC counts and percentages, projected age-eligible SOC siblings, and available elementary classrooms.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document and authorship.** "Recommendations for Schools of Choice, 2021-2022 School Year" is a board presentation by Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, and Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, bundled with a memorandum dated February 2, 2021 from Griffor and DiPilato to the TSD Board of Education under the subject "Schools of Choice Recommendations for the 2021-2022 School Year." It was carried on the February 23, 2021 board agenda as an updated version.

**Program framing.** Schools of Choice provides non-resident students with additional enrollment opportunities; participation in Schools of Choice is optional for districts; and the degree and extent of participation are determined at the local level, including application enrollment dates, grade levels and building assignment.

**Elementary enrollment projections from Plante Moran Cresa.** The presentation compares the firm's "Most Likely" projection with actual enrollment for Kindergarten and First Grade. For 2018/2019 the Kindergarten projection was 861 against an actual 849, and First Grade 914 against 915. For 2019/2020 the Kindergarten projection was 835 against 838, and First Grade 891 against 888. For 2020/2021 the Kindergarten projection was 844 against an actual 761 as of 1/28/21, and First Grade 884 against 829 as of 1/28/21. For 2021/2022 the projections are 845 for Kindergarten and 851 for First Grade, with actuals not yet known.

**Elementary SOC application and enrollment history.** A fifteen-year table reports openings advertised and applications received for Kindergarten and First Grade. Openings advertised were 25 and 25 in 2006-2007; 40 and 10 in 2007-2008; 30 and 5 in 2008-2009; 55 and 20 in 2009-2010; 100 and 50 in 2010-2011; 160 and 30 in 2011-2012; 100 and 30 in 2012-2013; 100 and 30 in 2013-2014; 50 and 25 in 2014-2015; 100 and 50 in 2015-2016; 100 and 30 in 2016-2017; 55 and 5 in 2017-2018; 40 and 3 in 2018-2019; 50 and 1 in 2019-2020; and 30 and 1 in 2020-2021. Applications received were 72 and 42 in 2006-2007; 92 and 35 in 2007-2008; 95 and 29 in 2008-2009; 84 and 47 in 2009-2010; 132 and 40 in 2010-2011; 142 and 53 in 2011-2012; 188 and 39 in 2012-2013; 183 and 61 in 2013-2014; 133 and 55 in 2014-2015; 156 and 40 in 2015-2016; 165 and 34 in 2016-2017; 150 and 41 in 2017-2018; 133 and 35 in 2018-2019; 143 and 17 in 2019-2020; and 91 and 12 in 2020-2021. Enrolled students in the most recent years were 48 Kindergarten and 1 First Grade in 2018-2019, 46 and 1 in 2019-2020, and 25 and 1 in 2020-2021. The table's TOTAL row reports 1035 Kindergarten and 315 First Grade openings advertised, 1959 and 580 applications received, and 1060 and 268 students enrolled.

**Charted distributions.** Two bar charts display Schools of Choice students in elementary buildings for the 2020-2021 school year, with a vertical axis running to 70, and Schools of Choice students district-wide by grade level for 2020-2021, with a vertical axis running to 160 and categories spanning grades 0 through 12.

**Elementary SOC versus non-SOC by building, 2020-2021.** Barnard Elementary had 42 SOC and 439 non-SOC students, 8.73% SOC, a change of -2.38%. Bemis Elementary had 6 and 499, 1.19%, -0.33%. Costello Elementary had 42 and 365, 10.32%, -2.28%. Hamilton Elementary had 34 and 429, 7.34%, -0.26%. Hill Elementary had 63 and 275, 18.64%, -0.87% - the highest SOC share of any building. Leonard Elementary had 36 and 395, 8.35%, -0.23%. Martell Elementary had 21 and 366, 5.43%, -0.68%. Morse Elementary had 7 and 425, 1.62%, -1.22%. Schroeder Elementary had 1 and 477, 0.21%, 0.02%. Troy Union Elementary had 16 and 431, 3.58%, -0.08%. TSD Preschool had 0 and 32, 0%, NA. Wass Elementary had 44 and 357, 10.97%, 0.31%. Wattles Elementary had 14 and 411, 3.29%, -0.10%. The totals are 326 SOC and 4901 non-SOC students, 6.24%, a change of -0.67%.

**By grade level.** Developmental Kindergarten had 0 SOC and 32 non-SOC students. Kindergarten had 27 and 702, 3.70%, -1.79%. First grade had 45 and 785, 5.42%, 0.04%. Second grade had 43 and 822, 4.97%, 0.50%. Third grade had 42 and 868, 4.62%, -4.11%. Fourth grade had 80 and 877, 8.36%, -1.37%. Fifth grade had 89 and 815, 9.85%, 2.37%. Totals again are 326 and 4901, 6.24%, -0.67%.

**Subgroup composition.** English Learners numbered 53 among SOC students, 16.26% with a change of -2.84%, and 1286 among non-SOC students, 26.24% with a change of -2.89%. Free/Reduced Lunch students numbered 60 among SOC students, 18.40%, -1.23%, and 632 among non-SOC students, 12.90%, 0.16%. Special Education students numbered 25 among SOC students, 7.67%, 0.51%, and 421 among non-SOC students, 8.59%, -0.45%.

**Ethnicity.** Among SOC students: Asian 70, 21.47%, change 1.05%; Black 19, 5.83%, -0.27%; Hawaiian/Pacific Islander 2, 0.61%, 0.08%; Hispanic 13, 3.99%, 0.54%; Multi-ethnic 18, 5.52%, -0.58%; Native American 0, 0.00%, 0.00%; White 204, 62.58%, -0.82%; total 326, 100%. Among non-SOC students: Asian 2048, 41.79%, 0.31%; Black 191, 3.90%, -0.18%; Hawaiian/Pacific Islander 14, 0.29%, 0.03%; Hispanic 217, 4.43%, 0.29%; Multi-ethnic 195, 3.98%, 0.34%; Native American 2, 0.04%, -0.04%; White 2234, 45.58%, -0.75%; total 4901, 100%.

**Kindergarten and First Grade enrollment history.** The presentation lists district Kindergarten and First Grade counts by year: 2008-2009, 775 and 830; 2009-2010, 739 and 817; 2010-2011, 752 and 785; 2011-2012, 727 and 832; 2012-2013, 768 and 795; 2013-2014, 766 and 814; 2014-2015, 700 and 787; 2015-2016, 755 and 728; 2016-2017, 798 and 769; 2017-2018, 812 and 845; 2018-2019, 800 and 871; 2019-2020, 792 and 845; and 2020-2021, 734 and 785, with the Kindergarten figure noted as including PreK (Developmental Kindergarten).

**Non-Schools of Choice students by grade, 2020-2021.** Kindergarten 734 (including PreK/Dev Kindergarten), 1st 785, 2nd 822, 3rd 868, 4th 877, 5th 815, 6th 823, 7th 900, 8th 952, 9th 962, 10th 957, 11th 942 and 12th 982, for a stated TOTAL of 11,419.

**Projected sibling preference placement.** A survey was emailed to current Schools of Choice families requesting information on siblings who would be eligible for Kindergarten, First Grade, and sixth, seventh and eighth grade for the 2021-2022 school year. The responses identify 10 Kindergarten students planning to attend, 1 First Grade student, and 9 Middle School students across sixth, seventh and eighth grade combined.

**Factors considered.** The February 2, 2021 memorandum lists the factors weighed in framing the recommendation: current enrollment across the Troy School District; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; the projected number of Schools of Choice siblings who would be age-eligible to enter the district in 2021-2022 if a decision is made to admit a "Limited" number of kindergarten, first and sixth through eighth grade students under Schools of Choice; and available elementary classrooms.

**Recommendations.** After analyzing that data, the administration recommends that the district use Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projection numbers as the foundation for determining the number of Schools of Choice students to admit for the 2021-2022 school year; accept SOC applications for 50 Kindergarten, 50 First Grade and 20 Middle School students, noting that based on the number of kindergarten applications received for the 2020-2021 school year the district anticipates attracting many more than 50 applicants, which would allow the district to admit 50 kindergarteners initially with the option of admitting additional students, if space allows, in the third week of August; and place middle school students in a building according to available space.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Troy School District's Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 states the district's middle school philosophy, nine program goals, five graduate outcomes, and the complete course catalog for grades 6, 7 and 8. Sixth graders take five academic classes plus required every-other-day physical education, while seventh and eighth graders take four academic classes plus required half-year Health/Physical Education and Digital Applications 1.0. Algebra 1 Honors, Geometry Honors and World Language I are taken in eighth grade, each earning high school credit and counting toward the high school GPA. The 18-page guide also catalogs more than two dozen half-year and full-year electives in visual art, music, computer science, engineering, media and life skills.

**Publication**
Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide, 2024-2025, 18 pages, presented to the Board of Education on February 11, 2025.

**Philosophy and Goals**
Troy middle schools provide a program that recognizes, accepts, respects and meets the diverse needs of young adolescents, characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation; a shared vision fostering respect for learning, diversity and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and community. Nine goals are listed, covering developmentally appropriate programs, meeting the needs of a diverse student population, core-subject skills and knowledge, discovery of special interests and aptitudes, diversified cultural/social/civic/vocational/recreational experiences, guidance services promoting self-esteem and responsible behavior, community partnerships, transition from elementary to high school, and modeling healthy lifestyles.

**Outcomes**
Five student outcomes: a self-directed learner, a quality worker, a positive communicator, a collaborative and cooperative contributor, and an involved and visionary citizen.

**Three-Year Overview**

| Grade | Academic load | Additional requirements |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Five academic classes | Physical Education EOD required; music students may add Orchestra EOD, Choir EOD, Band EOD, Art EOD |
| 7 | Four academic classes | Health/Physical Education half year; Digital Applications 1.0 half year; music option of Concert Band, Chamber Orchestra or Choir full year; elective total of one full year |
| 8 | Four academic classes | Music option of Symphonic Band, Advanced Orchestra or Choir full year; elective total of one full year for music students, two full-year classes for non-music students |

EOD is defined as Every Other Day.

**Grade 6 Courses**
Required: ELA 6, Language Arts 6, Mathematics 6 (or another math class), Physical Education 6, Science 6, Social Studies 6. Mathematics 6 is organized into ten units: Area and Surface Area; Introducing Ratios; Linear Relationships; Unit Rates and Percentages; Dividing Fractions; Arithmetic in Base Ten; Expressions and Equations; Rational Numbers; Data Sets and Distributions; Putting it all Together. Grade 6 electives meet every other day alternating with PE: Art 6, Band 6 or Orchestra 6, and 6th Grade Choir.

**Grade 7 Courses**
Digital Applications 1.0 (half year, required), English 7, Health and Physical Education 7 (half year, a ten-week course covering nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality and choosing healthy behaviors, with parental excusal permitted), Mathematics 7, Science 7, and Social Studies 7, which surveys ancient world history and geography from the beginning until around 1500.

**Grade 8 Courses**
Algebra 1 Honors (five critical areas), English 8, Geometry Honors (six critical areas), Mathematics 8, Science 8, and United States History 8, which surveys U.S. history from the time of the Native Americans to 1877. Algebra 1 Honors and Geometry Honors count toward high school credit and the high school GPA.

**Electives**
Half-year electives for grades 7 and 8: 2D Visual Art, 3D Visual Art, Applied Engineering, Art Expressions, Ceramics, Communication Arts, Computer Programming, Computer Science Discoveries, Creation Lab, Digital Applications 2.0, Innovation Incubator, Life Skills, LINKS (teacher recommendation only), Money Matters, Science and Engineering Explorations, Theatre Arts, Video Technology, and Video Technology 2. Grade 7 full-year electives: Chamber Orchestra, Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band, Graphic Design/Yearbook. Grade 8 electives: 7th/8th Choir, Advanced Orchestra, Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Jazz Band, Physical Education, Symphonic Band, WEB Leadership, and World Language I in Chinese I, French I, German I, Japanese I and Spanish I.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 is an 18-page publication appearing on the Board of Education agenda of February 11, 2025. It opens with the district's middle school philosophy: Troy middle schools provide a program that creates an environment recognizing, accepting, respecting and meeting the diverse needs and characteristics of young adolescent students, committed to academic excellence and to being developmentally responsive to adolescents' innate curiosity, desire to expand their environment, and need for recognition and personal achievement. The program is characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation that is challenging, integrative and exploratory; a shared vision with all members of the educational community fostering respect for learning, diversity and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and community members.

Nine Middle School Goals are enumerated. Goal 1: all programs will be developmentally appropriate. Goal 2: ensure all programs meet the needs of a diverse student population. Goal 3: ensure all students develop skills and knowledge in the core subject areas. Goal 4: provide opportunity to discover special interests, attitudes, aptitudes and abilities. Goal 5: provide diversified experiences in cultural, social, civic, vocational and recreational programs. Goal 6: provide guidance services and programs promoting self-esteem, independence and responsible behavior. Goal 7: provide opportunity to establish partnerships with the community. Goal 8: provide a transition from elementary to high school. Goal 9: provide a model for healthy lifestyles.

Five Middle School Outcomes follow: a self-directed learner who is responsible, enthusiastic, thinks independently and is open-minded and intellectually curious; a quality worker who designs a plan, applies resources, technologies and organizational strategies, creates products and performances, monitors development, maintains high standards and assesses results; a positive communicator; a collaborative and cooperative contributor who creates and sustains productive group relationships, respects the contributions of others, helps resolve conflicts and stays focused and task oriented; and an involved and visionary citizen who develops awareness of global issues, contributes to local and world communities, advocates for the environment and prepares to meet future challenges.

The three-year middle school overview specifies that all sixth graders take five academic classes; seventh and eighth graders each take four academic classes. Sixth grade requires Physical Education on an every-other-day (EOD) basis for both music and non-music students, with Orchestra EOD, Choir EOD, Band EOD and Art EOD listed as the alternating options. Seventh grade requires Health/Physical Education for a half year and Digital Applications 1.0 for a half year, plus, for music students, one of Concert Band (full year), Chamber Orchestra (full year) or Choir (full year); the elective load totals one full year, taken as two half-year classes or one full-year class. Eighth grade music students choose among Symphonic Band (full year), Advanced Orchestra (full year) and Choir (full year); non-music eighth graders carry an elective total of two full-year classes, taken as four half-year classes, two half-year classes plus one full-year class, or two full-year classes.

Grade 6 required courses are ELA 6 (full year), which studies literature of various genres and informational text including literary nonfiction with emphasis on inference from textual evidence, thematic and character development, claims and evidence, academic vocabulary and independent choice reading; Language Arts 6 (full year), covering narrative, informational and argumentative writing using mentor texts and the writing process; Mathematics 6 (full year, or another math class), covering ratio and rate, dividing fractions by fractions, negative numbers and variables; Physical Education 6 (full year EOD), run either as a yearlong every-other-day program or an everyday semester class; Science 6 (full year), with units on cells and heredity, ecology, Earth's changing surface, and species adaptation and survival; and Social Studies 6 (full year), a geography-based course covering physical and human geography, migration and settlement, culture and cultural diffusion, population and demographic changes, resource use, and trade and economic interdependence. Mathematics 6 lists ten units: Unit 1 Area and Surface Area; Unit 2 Introducing Ratios; Unit 3 Linear Relationships; Unit 4 Unit Rates and Percentages; Unit 5 Dividing Fractions; Unit 6 Arithmetic in Base Ten; Unit 7 Expressions and Equations; Unit 8 Rational Numbers; Unit 9 Data Sets and Distributions; Unit 10 Putting it all Together.

Grade 6 elective courses meet every other day, alternating with PE: Art 6 (full year EOD), Band 6 or Orchestra 6 (full year EOD, with fifth-grade band or orchestra or prior formal instruction expected), and 6th Grade Choir (full year EOD), which follows the National Core Arts Standards of Perform, Create, Respond and Connect.

Grade 7 required courses are Digital Applications 1.0 (half year), covering 21st Century and Web 2.0 online tools; English 7 (full year); Health and Physical Education 7 (half year), a combined ten-week course covering nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality and choosing healthy behaviors, with units countering messages encouraging tobacco, alcohol and other drug use and information on the spread of AIDS and sexually transmitted diseases, and with parents permitted to excuse their child from sessions on human sexuality and AIDS; Mathematics 7 (full year, or another math class), extending rates and ratios to proportional relationships and all rational numbers; Science 7 (full year), covering Earth's waters, weather and climate, astronomy, waves, energy, physical and chemical changes, and chemical properties; and Social Studies 7 (full year), focused on ancient world history and geography with content literacy, investigating human history from the beginning until around 1500.

Grade 8 courses are Algebra 1 Honors (full year, or another math class), a first-year high school algebra course for advanced students with five critical areas covering linear equations and inequalities, functions and sequences, regression techniques, exponential/quadratic/rational equations and systems, and specialized functions including absolute value, step and piecewise-defined; English 8 (full year); Geometry Honors (full year, or another math class) for advanced students who have completed Algebra 1 Honors, with six critical areas covering congruence and rigid motions, similarity and right triangle trigonometry, coordinate geometry, circles, geometric measurement in two and three dimensions, and geometric modeling; Mathematics 8 (full year, or another math class), covering linear relationships, linear equations in one and two variables, functions and irrational numbers; Science 8 (full year), covering energy, biogeochemical cycles, resources and human impacts, the rock cycle, Earth's interior, plate tectonics, earthquakes, volcanoes, hydrogeology, severe weather, Earth in space, the sun, Earth history and geologic time and climate change, including an online Moodle project; and United States History 8 (full year), surveying U.S. history from the time of the Native Americans to 1877, with detailed study of the American Revolution, formation of the national government, westward movement, and the Civil War and Reconstruction, and periodic study of Michigan history and U.S. foreign affairs. Both Algebra 1 Honors and Geometry Honors count toward high school credit and are figured into the high school GPA.

Half-year elective courses for grades 7 and 8 are 2D Visual Art; 3D Visual Art (papier-mache, clay, batik and mixed media); Applied Engineering (stress analysis, mechanical engineering, renewable energy systems, aerodynamics, space and rocketry); Art Expressions; Ceramics (pinch, coil and slab construction); Communication Arts (public speaking, pantomime, roleplaying, interviews, listening skills, improvisation); Computer Programming (Introduction to JavaScript: Drawing and Animation, JavaScript: Games and Visualizations, HTML/CSS: Making Webpages, HTML/JS: Making Webpages Interactive, plus building and programming a robot); Computer Science Discoveries; Creation Lab (bridge building, soldering, coding, game creation, projectiles, S.T.E.A.M. focus); Digital Applications 2.0 (Adobe Creative Suite, video production, animation, digital imaging, Dreamweaver; prerequisite is successful completion of Digital Applications 1.0); Innovation Incubator, whose cornerstone is the Larson Innovation Shark Tank project in which teams pitch inventions to members of the Metro Detroit business community including market researchers, patent attorneys and engineers; Life Skills (food preparation and hand and machine sewing); LINKS, a peer-to-peer support program pairing general education students with students with Autism Spectrum Disorder and other special needs, by teacher recommendation only; Money Matters (Michigan Career Pathways, budgets, bank accounts, credit, interest, investing and responsible spending); Science and Engineering Explorations, which prepares work for competitions such as the Science and Engineering Fair of Metro Detroit (SEFMD); Theatre Arts, which includes a public performance; Video Technology, using Windows Movie Maker and Apple iMovie with live morning news broadcasts and media literacy and copyright ethics; and Video Technology 2.

Grade 7 full-year electives are Chamber Orchestra, Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band, and Graphic Design/Yearbook, the latter connecting students with the Boulan Park School Community. Grade 8 electives are 7th/8th Choir, Advanced Orchestra (which requires many evening performances plus a Saturday performance at the MSBOA Orchestra Festival), Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Jazz Band (by audition or teacher approval, with members also participating in a concert band ensemble), Physical Education, Symphonic Band (requiring many evening performances plus two Saturday performances including MSBOA Band Festival), WEB Leadership (Where Everyone Belongs, covering sixth grade orientation, school character and culture programs, charity opportunities and student mentoring), and World Language I. World Language I is a full-year, every-day course counting toward high school credit and the high school GPA, offered in Chinese I, French I, German I, Japanese I and Spanish I; the guide warns the class may only be offered at the high school during 1st hour, that parents would need to provide transportation to the high school, and that a shuttle will bring students back to the middle school.

Rooms 22 (Math), 30 (ELA) and 36 (Social Studies) each receive a specified list of flexible, mostly caster-mounted seating, tables, markerboards and storage from Steelcase, Smith System, Flowform, Groove, Flavors, Numbers, Elemental, Interchange, Constellate and Silhouette product lines, with additional Orangebox lounge and bench pieces proposed for the cafeteria, media center and corridor. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education's combined annual organizational and regular meeting held remotely via Zoom Webinar on January 19, 2021, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:06 p.m. and adjourned at 9:22 p.m. with roughly 275 additional audience members present. The Board re-elected Schmidt president (6-1, Hammond opposed), Wilson vice president, Hauff secretary, and appointed Rick L. West treasurer, then adopted resolutions on fund depositories, legal counsel, meeting schedule and committee assignments. On a 5-2 vote it authorized the Superintendent to amend the Robertson Brothers Co. purchase agreement for the Square Lake Road surplus land sold for $1,425,000.00.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education, Troy, Michigan. Board meeting minutes for January 19, 2021, held remotely via Zoom Webinar after public notice permitting remote community participation. Called to order by President Schmidt at 7:06 p.m.; adjourned at 9:22 p.m. Minutes signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary (GNH/jh).

**Attendance**
Board members present by Zoom videoconference from locations in Troy, Michigan: Schmidt, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson. Also present: Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Moynihan, Carson, Zawislak, Harris and West; Dana Abrahams of Clark Hill, P.C.; two Student Board Reps; approximately 275 additional audience members.

**Student representatives**
Nathania Nartey (Athens High School) and Pranay Gupta (International Academy-East) reported. Sejal Patil (Troy High School) and Carlton Thomas (Troy College & Career High School) were not in attendance.

**Organizational actions**

| Item | Action | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 21-002 | Schmidt as acting chairperson (Philippart/Wilson) | 7-0 |
| -- | Judy Holmes appointed temporary secretary | -- |
| 21-003 | Schmidt president through December 31, 2021 (Hauff/Anne) | 6 yes; 1 no (Hammond) |
| 21-004 | Wilson vice president through December 31, 2021 (Philippart/Anne) | 7-0 |
| 21-005 | Hauff secretary through December 31, 2021 (Hammond/Philippart) | 7-0 |
| 21-006 | Rick L. West, Assistant Superintendent Business Services, appointed Treasurer January-December 2021 (Philippart/Anne) | 7-0 |
| 21-007 | Fund Depositories and Investments resolution (Philippart/Hammond) | 7-0 |
| 21-008 | Legal counsel designations for calendar 2021 (Anne/Philippart) | 7-0 |
| 21-009 | Superintendent designated Deputy Secretary for 2021 (Hammond/Hauff) | 7-0 |
| 21-010 | Judy Holmes designated to post meeting notices for 2021 (Wilson/Hauff) | 7-0 |
| 21-011 | 2021 calendar-year meeting schedule (Anne/Philippart) | 7-0 |
| 21-012 | 2021 Board Committee Memberships (Hauff/Philippart) | 7-0 |

**Depositories**
Bank of America, Charter One Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, PFM Securities, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank, and PNC Bank. Investments follow Board Policy 5000.06 and Section 380.1223(1)(h) of the Revised School Code.

**Recognition**
Mission Moment honoring six LERN (Leading for Equity Design Network) student teammates, part of the National Equity Project; presented by Assistant Superintendent DiPilato and Troy High Assistant Principal Brian Zawislak. January is School Board Appreciation Month; trustees received a long-sleeved oneTROY pullover.

**Public communication**
Tony Lucchi (TEA President), Jason Cichowicz (TEA representative, 5th grade teacher at Schroeder Elementary) and Jeff Rainwater (teacher, Troy College and Career High School) addressed the Board on the safety and timing of returning teachers and students to buildings.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Convening.** The Troy Board of Education met on January 19, 2021 remotely via Zoom Webinar, with public notice posted so community members could participate remotely. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:06 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson were present via Zoom videoconference, each connecting from Troy, Michigan and each stating name and location for the roll. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Moynihan, Carson, Zawislak, Harris and West; Dana Abrahams from Clark Hill, P.C.; two Student Board Reps; and approximately 275 additional members of the audience. Mr. Schmidt explained that this meeting is where the Board elects officers, appoints committee members for the upcoming year and approves or authorizes items considered on an annual basis, with the regular Board meeting following the organizational portion.

**Student representatives.** Because student representatives needed to prepare for mid-terms, they reported first. Nathania Nartey, Student Representative for Athens High School, and Pranay Gupta, Student Representative for the International Academy-East, shared updates. Sejal Patil, Student Representative for Troy High School, and Carlton Thomas, Student Representative for Troy College & Career High School, were not in attendance.

**Officer elections.** Resolution 21-002: moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Dr. Wilson that Mr. Schmidt serve as acting chairperson until election of a president; roll call 7 yes, 0 no. Mr. Schmidt then appointed Judy Holmes to act as temporary secretary until election of the Board secretary. Resolution 21-003: Mr. Hauff nominated Mr. Schmidt for president; nominations closed on a motion by Dr. Wilson supported by Dr. Philippart, 7 yes, 0 no; the resolution that Mr. Schmidt serve as president until December 31, 2021 was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne and carried 6 yes (Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb) to 1 no (Hammond). Resolution 21-004: Dr. Philippart nominated Dr. Wilson for vice president; nominations closed 7 yes, 0 no; the resolution that Dr. Wilson serve as vice president until December 31, 2021 was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne, carrying 7 yes, 0 no. Resolution 21-005: Mrs. Hammond nominated Mr. Hauff for secretary; nominations closed 7 yes, 0 no; the resolution that Mr. Hauff serve as secretary until December 31, 2021 was moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Dr. Philippart, carrying 7 yes, 0 no.

**Treasurer.** Resolution 21-006, moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne, appointed Rick L. West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, as Treasurer of the Troy Board of Education for the period January through December 2021. Roll call 7 yes, 0 no.

**Fund depositories and investments.** Resolution 21-007, moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Hammond, adopted the resolution on Fund Depositories and Investments for January through December 2021 and directed that the attached resolution be incorporated in its entirety into the official minutes. The resolution recites that public monies, including tax monies, coming into the hands of Rick West, Treasurer of Troy School District, are to be deposited or invested in his name as Treasurer with the following institutions: Bank of America, Charter One Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, PFM Securities, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank, and PNC Bank. Monies may be withdrawn by checks signed with the facsimile signature of Treasurer Rick West, and in emergencies the handwritten signature of Rick West or of Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, who may sign on the General Fund account and the Payroll account at Bank of America. Accounts established at PNC Bank for paying Troy Career Center expenses may be drawn on by checks with the handwritten signature of the Troy Career Center Manager, Assistant Manager, or Program Coordinators. The account established at Comerica Bank for paying health care and dependent care flexible spending claims may be drawn by ACH debit to Next Generation Enrollment, Inc. or by checks with the Treasurer's facsimile signature. The Treasurer may open or close accounts with the listed institutions when in the District's interest; funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06; and the Treasurer is authorized to combine money from more than one fund for an investment authorized by subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code, with the maximum amount to be invested regulated by the school code. The certification is signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary of Troy School District, Oakland County, Michigan, given under hand and seal this 19th day of January 2021. Roll call 7 yes, 0 no.

**Legal counsel.** Resolution 21-008, moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart, continued the designation of Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Miller Johnson; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; Beier Howlett, P.C.; and Miller Canfield P.L.C. as legal counsel to advise or represent the Troy School District and Board of Education as necessary for the 2021 calendar year, with the Superintendent authorized to consult additional counsel as needed with prior notification to the Board. Mr. Gottlieb stated that he feels it is critical to have dialogue and discourse with the various law firms the district engages. Roll call 7 yes, 0 no.

**Other annual designations.** Resolution 21-009, moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mr. Hauff, continued the designation of the Superintendent of Schools as Deputy Secretary of the Board with authority to act for the secretary for calendar 2021; 7 yes, 0 no. Resolution 21-010, moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff, designated Judy Holmes, Secretary to the Superintendent of Schools, as the person for posting notices of meetings for 2021; 7 yes, 0 no. Resolution 21-011, moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart, adopted the schedule of meetings for the 2021 calendar year as shown on the attached calendar; 7 yes, 0 no. Resolution 21-012, moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Dr. Philippart, adopted the Board Committee Memberships for the 2021 school year as attached; 7 yes, 0 no.

**Recognition: LERN Network student teammates.** As the evening's Mission Moment the Board recognized six students serving on the LERN Network. Mrs. DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, explained that LERN is the Leading for Equity Design Network, part of the National Equity Project (NEP) with which the Troy School District has been working, and that the team is made up of faculty, teachers, administrators and student representatives. She introduced Troy High School Assistant Principal Brian Zawislak, the team's student liaison, who noted the six student leaders joined LERN in December and introduced Sarayu Bethamcharla (Troy High), Kian Schneeweis (Baker Middle School), Gianna Pearson (Athens High School) and Wamucie Karimi (Troy High). Noah Veen (Troy College & Career High School) and Erik Schmidt (Athens) are also LERN student representatives but were unable to attend. Students described wanting to lift the power of student voice around diversity, inclusion and equity; one student shared a challenge experienced in school and how he overcame it.

**Board Recognition Month.** Each January the Troy School District honors the trustees of its Board of Education. School Board Appreciation Month recognizes the role trustees play in reinforcing the mission of the Troy School District, ensuring learning for all, through policies, fiscal stewardship and support of teaching and learning. As a symbol of appreciation the District presented each trustee a long-sleeved oneTROY pullover.

**Additions and deletions; public communication.** There were no additions or deletions. Under public communication on non-agenda items, Tony Lucchi, President of the Troy Education Association (TEA), addressed the Board about having teachers return to buildings for in-seat and hybrid instruction during the pandemic, discussing safety issues and the need for teachers to be vaccinated before returning. Jason Cichowicz, TEA representative and 5th grade teacher at Schroeder Elementary, addressed the safety of returning teachers and students and the inequity of elementary schedules compared to secondary. Jeff Rainwater, teacher at Troy College and Career High School, addressed returning to in-seat instruction too soon and how having COVID in the fall affected him and his family. A later public communication period drew no speakers.

**Consent agenda.** Resolution 21-013, moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Hammond, approved items A through G: corrections to the November Workshop and Meeting Minutes to include the location where Board members participated remotely; minutes of the December 1, 2020 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the December 15, 2020 Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the December 18, 2020 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the December 18, 2020 Closed Session Meeting; Treasurer's Report for November 2020; and appointment of the Board Negotiating Team for TEA Contract Negotiations. Roll call 7 yes, 0 no.

**Business items.** Resolution 21-014 (Roofing), moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Hauff, awarded the bid roof replacement and approved the amount as an expenditure of the Capital Projects & Building Site Sinking Funds; roll call 7 yes, 0 no. Resolution 21-015 (Site Work - Paving), moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart, awarded the bid Site Work Paving Program and approved the amount as an expenditure of the Capital Projects & Building Site Sinking Funds; roll call 7 yes, 0 no.

**Section 1 Purchase Agreement Amendment.** Resolution 21-016 was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Hauff. It recites that the School District passed a resolution on April 21, 2020 authorizing the sale of surplus real property in the City of Troy, Oakland County, Michigan, described as 6.12 +/- acres of vacant land located on the North side of Square Lake Road, East of John R Road, the Premises being part of a larger 70.647 +/- acre parcel (Parcel 2), with the District additionally including an 11.281 +/- acre parcel (Parcel 1); the undeveloped portion of Parcel 2 and all of Parcel 1 are to remain preserved in perpetuity through a conservation easement. In compliance with that resolution the Superintendent negotiated and executed an offer to purchase dated June 8, 2020 with Robertson Brothers Co., on behalf of an entity to be formed, to purchase the Premises for One Million Four Hundred Twenty Five Thousand and 00/100 ($1,425,000.00) Dollars with an earnest money deposit of Fifty Thousand and 00/100 ($50,000.00) Dollars. The District and Purchaser then learned that up to an additional 6.29 acres of land must be deeded to the Purchaser to obtain the density bonus assumed in the Purchaser's Concept Plan under the City's One-Family Cluster Option Ordinance, which Concept Plan was incorporated by reference into the Purchase Agreement. The amendment would deed the additional acreage at Closing while making clear the additional acreage remains preserved as open space in perpetuity except for the storm pond/basin, the trailhead gravel parking lot and other similar requirements necessary for the proposed development. The resolution authorizes the Superintendent or his designee to negotiate the amendment, adjust Purchase Agreement timelines, and execute the amendment and all documents incidental to the sale after consultation with legal counsel. Board members, administration and attorney Dana Abrahams discussed the topic. Roll call: 5 yes (Anne, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson), 2 no (Gottlieb, Hammond).

**COVID-19 plan reconfirmation.** Under Other, the Extended Learning Plan was listed. Dr. Machesky shared information about the most recent COVID case numbers in Michigan and Oakland County, encouraged the community to visit the District's website for updated COVID data, and stated that no changes were being recommended at that time to the Return to Learn Plan. Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142 provides a structure for schools planning a return of Pre-K through Post High School education, requiring Michigan districts to adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan addressing the phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan, to submit a reconfirmation plan to the Board monthly, and to post the Preparedness Plan on the district website home page. Resolution 21-017, moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff, approved the District's Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan; roll call 6 yes (Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb), 1 no (Hammond).

**Adjournment.** The meeting was adjourned at 9:22 p.m. Minutes respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the notation GNH/jh.
