https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**What the excerpt is.** Four consecutive candidate profiles from the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) 2021 election booklet, all for the Region 8 seat carrying a Three-Year Term on the MASB Board of Directors. Running heads alternate between "Candidates for MASB Board of Directors" (pages 22 and 24) and "2021 Elections" (pages 23 and 25). Each profile follows the same template: candidate name, district and county, time served on that board, offices held, MASB certification awards, and an election statement. Three of the four candidates come from Oakland County districts and one from Macomb County. The item appears on the Troy Board of Education's February 23, 2021 agenda.

**Sandra Dukhie, Ferndale Public Schools, Oakland County.** Time served on the board: four years. Offices held: Vice President. Her election statement opens on the theme that education is said to be the great equalizer but has struggled to level the playing field since the very beginning, and that board members are positioned to set education on a path to excellence for all by way of equity and inclusion. She writes that her passion combined with her experience make her an exceptional candidate, and that diversity, equity and inclusion work is necessary and imperative. Serving as a school board member challenges her to look at all decisions crossing the Board table through an equity lens, which led to her co-authoring her district's resolution declaring racism as a public health crisis. She is an active member and participant of the Oakland County Council for Diversity Equity and Inclusion. In the summer preceding the booklet she hosted and facilitated a 30-Day Racial Equity Habit Building Challenge via social media, adapted from Eddie Moore Jr.'s 21-day challenge. She has worked in public education since 1999 and has been an active parent in the education of her five sons, which led her to seek a board seat for her school district. She was appointed to the Ferndale School Board in March of 2017 and then elected to her current term in the November 2018 election. Community members selected her to chair the Ferndale Inclusion Network, an organization whose mission is intent on building a more diverse and inclusive community. She states she would like to serve on the MASB Board of Directors because she believes she will bring a different perspective and a much needed lens on equity and inclusion.

**Mary Hanser, Oxford Community Schools, Oakland County.** Time served on the board: two years. MASB certification: Award of Merit and Certified Boardmember Award; no offices held are listed. Her election statement says she wishes to serve on the MASB Board to actively advocate for and support Region 8 districts and to work with other school board members to make Michigan a public school destination, because of equitable funding and educational opportunities, well trained and knowledgeable school boards, and honoring the value of every single student and staff member. She describes herself as relatively new in the school board world, bringing a forward thinking perspective. She currently serves on the Oakland County School Board Association (OCSBA) Diversity, Equity & Inclusion Committee and the OCSBA Government Relations Committee. Within her first two years of board service she earned her CBA Certification and Award of Merit and recently completed the coursework for the Advocacy Skills Specialty. Her previous service to the community includes high school robotics team mentor, FIRST Robotics Competition volunteer, and the Macomb County Commission on Women. Her background is in business; she earned a Bachelor of Business Administration degree from Walsh College and has worked in the non-profit sector as well as in the corporate world and small business.

**Birgit McQuiston, Lake Orion Community Schools, Oakland County.** Time served on the board: nine years. Offices held: Vice President and Secretary. MASB certification: Award of Merit, Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember Award, Master Diamond Award, and Certified Boardmember Award. She was first elected to the Lake Orion Board of Education in May of 2011; her passion for education was ignited as she volunteered in her children's classroom and grew as she worked on School Improvement Teams and the District Improvement Team. She ran for the board of education in order to preserve the integrity of the work of the board. Her board work includes the policy, curriculum, board self-assessment, superintendent evaluation, and Lamp of Learning committees, as well as the Government Relations Committee and service as Diversity Equity and Inclusion Representative to the county association. She has served as president, vice president and secretary, and has traveled to Lansing to address the senate and house education committees to advocate for local control and against unfunded mandates. She was elected to her third term this past November. She became interested in the work of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) by attending meetings and broadened her professional development while connecting with other trustees; she is in her third year on the OCSBA Board of Directors, has been secretary for two years, and serves on the meeting planning committee, with a drive to help broaden the scope of the association's work with the 201 trustees of Oakland County, noting that even amidst a pandemic they are increasing opportunities to connect and to provide relevant professional development. Her pursuit of excellence led her to earn the Master Diamond Award in 2019, and she was appointed to the MASB Resolutions & Bylaws Committee in 2018. She is running for the MASB Board of Directors to be part of the ongoing work of developing board leaders and advocating for equitable and exceptional public education for all students, to help maintain the integrity of board work, and as a strong proponent of local control; she seeks to serve Region 8 as a visible and accessible director who will collaborate with all trustees in the region. She is a founding and current member of Blessings in a Backpack - Lake Orion, which provides weekend food for at-risk students facing food insecurity, and has been active within her community since March in helping provide resources and delivering food to community members at risk of food insecurity.

**Gina Walker, New Haven Community Schools, Macomb County.** Time served on the board: 10 years. Offices held: President. MASB certification: Award of Merit, Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember Award, Master Diamond Award, and Certified Boardmember Award. Her election statement notes she has served in an elected position in public education for 10 years, four of which she served as President of the New Haven Community Schools Board of Education. She is interested in helping provide opportunities for school board members on current challenges and obstacles facing public education, has been active in her county association as well as in MASB, and has earned the Master Diamond Award for education credits. She hopes to have a positive impact for both Region 8 and public education across the state, and welcomes the opportunity to bring back and share information to Region 8 as well as share ideas from her region with other members of the Board of Directors. She holds a Bachelor of Business Administration from Eastern Michigan University with a focus in Accounting and Internal Auditing.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Principal's report presented to the Troy Board of Education on June 23, 2021 covering the International Academy's three campuses. It reports successful graduation ceremonies at West, Okma and East, and an IB examination session held April 29 through May 20 in which 326 students sat as full Diploma Program candidates, described as 94 percent of the graduating class. The report also sets the 2021-22 return-to-school calendar, announces an IB evaluation visit for November 10 through November 12, and summarizes a staff survey in which all three campuses chose Culture as the school goal to pursue next year.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Overview
Slide-style principal's report for the International Academy, presented at the Troy School District Board meeting of June 23, 2021. It covers end-of-year results, the coming IB evaluation, the 2021-22 opening calendar, a restructured school improvement committee, the four school goals, and verbatim staff survey comments.

Graduation
Ceremonies are reported as a success at all three campuses:

| Campus | Date | Location and time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| West | Wednesday, May 26 | Lakeland HS Fieldhouse, 7:00pm |
| Okma | Thursday, June 3 | BHHS Athletic Field, 7:00pm |
| East | Saturday, June 5 | DTE, 12:30pm |

IB examinations (April 29 to May 20)
The session is reported as a success. There were 326 full Diploma Program candidates, stated as 94 percent of the graduating class; 13 of those students will have one or more exams graded on the non-exam route because of quarantine or other illness. Another 18 were course candidates attempting HL credit, 1 student opted to return and take exams in November, and 8 students withdrew from all IB exams.

IB evaluation visit
Scheduled Wednesday, November 10 through Friday, November 12.

Return to school
Thursday, August 12 for new student orientation, new teacher orientation, and schedule pickup with school photos; Monday, August 16 for staff professional development; Tuesday, August 17 as the first day of school for students; Friday, August 27 no school.

Tri-Campus School Improvement Committee
The report proposes reinstituting a tri-campus School Improvement Committee that is both school wide and campus specific. Its responsibilities would be to prepare for IB evaluation visits, meet state professional development requirements, and develop professional development for staff.

School goals
Instruction: instruction will be engaging, innovative, student-centered and inquiry based, with the goal of promoting and supporting effective and innovative pedagogy in the classroom. Curriculum: the curriculum will be in full alignment with the standards of the International Baccalaureate Middle Years and Diploma Programs plus state standards, with interdisciplinary units fully implemented and assessed at all levels, a goal of two units per year for MYP, one each semester. Culture: the culture will balance the social, emotional and physical health of the community and embrace both commonalities and individuality, with goals to build capacity as a community cultivating a global culture of acceptance and inclusion and to foster a culture of service learning. Assessment: assessments will fairly evaluate diverse abilities, with formative assessment used for practice and feedback and summative assessment emphasizing mastery, and a goal of defining and aligning the assessment philosophy and policy within departments and school wide.

Staff survey
Asked which school goal to engage in for the 2021-22 school year, all three campuses chose Culture. Comments cite the need to rebuild culture after a year of uncertainty, student transition back to full face-to-face instruction, continued social-emotional support, and the view that culture is the foundation on which the other goals rest. Suggested secondary goals center on rethinking assessment, focusing on the Diploma Program, analyzing which pandemic-era instructional methods worked, and refining new DP curricula. Practices staff want to carry forward include asynchronous days, Canvas for organizing and collecting assignments, one-to-one device access, the House system and house competitions, the Open House video, and flexible time management. Staff also identified pre-COVID features they could do without, naming intense workload and stress levels and in-person conferences.

Mission statement
The report closes with the International Academy mission: through the International Baccalaureate program, instilling cultural appreciation and global citizenship while promoting personal development and a passion for learning.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Principal's report for the International Academy delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education at its June 23, 2021 meeting. The document is a slide deck covering the close of the 2020-21 school year and planning for 2021-22 across the Academy's three campuses, West, Okma and East.

Graduation. All three ceremonies are reported as a success. West held graduation Wednesday, May 26 at the Lakeland HS Fieldhouse at 7:00pm. Okma held graduation Thursday, June 3 at the BHHS Athletic Field at 7:00pm. East held graduation Saturday, June 5 at DTE at 12:30pm.

IB examinations. The exam window ran April 29 through May 20 and is likewise reported as a success. There were 326 full Diploma Program candidates, stated in the report as 94 percent of the graduating class. Of those, 13 students will have one or more of their exams graded on the non-exam route because of quarantine or other illness. A further 18 students sat as course candidates attempting HL credit. One student opted to return and take exams in November, and 8 students withdrew from all IB exams.

IB evaluation visit. The Academy will host an IB evaluation visit Wednesday, November 10 through Friday, November 12.

Return to school calendar. Thursday, August 12 is set for New Student Orientation, New Teacher Orientation, and Schedule Pickup and School Photos. Monday, August 16 is staff professional development. Tuesday, August 17 is the first day of school for students. Friday, August 27 is a no school day.

Tri-Campus School Improvement Committee. The report calls for reinstituting a tri-campus School Improvement Committee that operates both school wide and campus specific. Its stated responsibilities are to prepare for IB evaluation visits, address state professional development requirements, and develop professional development for staff.

School goals. Four goal areas are set out with accompanying statements.

Instruction. The instruction of the International Academy will be engaging, innovative, student-centered and inquiry based. The goal is to promote and support effective and innovative pedagogy in the classroom.

Curriculum. The curriculum of the International Academy will be in full alignment with the standards of the International Baccalaureate Middle Years and Diploma Programs in addition to state standards. The goal is that interdisciplinary units will be fully implemented and assessed at all levels, with a target of two units per year for MYP, one each semester.

Culture. The culture of the International Academy will balance the social, emotional and physical health of the community, and will embrace and value commonalities and individuality. Two goals are stated: continue to build capacity as a community that cultivates a global culture encouraging acceptance and inclusion, and foster and support a culture of service learning.

Assessment. Assessments will fairly evaluate the unique and diverse abilities and knowledge base of all students. Formative assessments will be used to strengthen skills and provide practice and feedback during the learning process, while summative assessments will emphasize mastery of the skills and content knowledge students have had an opportunity to learn. The goal is to define and align the assessment philosophy and policy within departments and as a school.

Staff survey and conversations, primary goal. Asked which school goal they would most like to engage in for the 2021-22 school year, all three campuses want to pursue Culture. Quoted staff responses include the observation that after a year of uncertainty the culture at IA will need rebuilding because students missed out on much of what makes the Academy distinctive; that IA has excellent educators who will adapt curriculum and instruction to make up for material not covered, but that the most important factors are the cultural pieces, including the culture of commitment to excelling, the culture derived from the Academy's international grounding, and the culture of interpersonal relationships many students have not been able to form; that culture is what students will be looking forward to when they return to full face-to-face instruction in the fall; that staff want to continue guiding students to succeed with the rigor of the IB program; that students and staff face a difficult transition back to real school and will need help balancing physical, emotional, educational and life stressors, with continued focus on SEL rather than a return to business as usual; that culture work is never done and there is much to do before changing priorities, since students will struggle to readjust next fall and supporting that transition should be the greatest priority; and that culture is the foundation upon which the others are built.

Staff survey, secondary goals. Responses on a secondary goal emphasize assessment and curriculum. Staff noted that the year forced a rethinking of assessment, with more creativity and less grade-driven work that was healthy for staff and students, and that high quality authentic assessments that do not overwhelm should continue. Working with digital assessments allowed work outside the box of what a typical summative and formative assessment looks like, prompting a desire to reevaluate assessment style going forward. Other comments call for spending time focusing on the Diploma Program; for more focus on in-person instruction after a year and a half on Zoom; for space and time to analyze which instructional methods introduced during the year worked and how they might improve overall instruction; for continued curriculum improvement, noting that large curricular hurdles were cleared during the year and that some choices favored ease during a stressful time over better curricular choices that now need correction; and for retaining classroom technologies, particularly methods that allowed more immediate feedback than traditional approaches, with interest in using them to differentiate assignments and assessments or to create a semi-self-paced course allowing more personal preference and interest. Additional responses ask for consistency between departments regarding assessment or a school-wide grading and percentage policy for tests, note that some teachers sit at polar ends of the assessment spectrum and that the whole staff should discuss the topic, and observe that new DP curricula in several subjects would benefit from extra time to iron out wrinkles.

Practices to carry forward and new ideas. Staff suggested exploring how asynchronous days could work, based on feedback gathered from numerous freshmen and sophomores met with during second semester, on the grounds that students and staff work very hard and would benefit from set-aside time. Continuing to use Canvas to organize and to an extent collect assignments was cited as useful, as was using Canvas to cut down on paper and communicate with absent students. Staff asked for easy and consistent student access to a device in class, describing one-to-one as a goal, and expressed enthusiasm for the House system, friendly house competitions and team building, more field trips after a year indoors, and connecting alumni with students. The Open House video was praised, and the picnic was reported to be better without grilling and with a focus on fun activities. Staff also valued professional consideration of time management, with flexibility to leave when not teaching or meeting described as crucial to mental health and to fulfilling work and home obligations, noting a high level of trust during the year that the job would get done.

Aspects of pre-COVID school life to do without. Staff named the intense workload and high levels of stress before COVID as detrimental to student and staff health, calling for additional and focused or protected time, and suggested that in-person conferences may not be necessary.

Additional comments. Staff asked that more teachers understand program expectations beyond their own disciplines, and suggested a workshop or professional development session on Canvas functionality since its many features can be confusing or unobvious to new users. Closing comments thank the principal for support and grace during a difficult year and for seeking staff input, express anticipation for the new school year, and state that culture and instruction are key to next year's success, with investment there also taking care of curriculum and assessments.

Mission. The report closes with the Academy's mission statement: the International Academy community, through the International Baccalaureate program, instills cultural appreciation and global citizenship while promoting personal development and a passion for learning.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A twenty-slide Troy School District presentation titled "TSD Equity & Inclusion," delivered as a Board of Education workshop on May 18, 2021, tracing the district's equity work from the 2009 TSD Diversity Study to a newly created Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion and Community Relationships position built around three priorities: Assess, Connect and Engage. The centerpiece finding is from the Equity & Inclusion Survey conducted by Hannover Research, which captured 7,448 stakeholder perceptions and identified the greatest opportunity for improvement in the perceptions and experiences of Black students and Black parents.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Framing**
Presented under the title "TSD Equity & Inclusion" as a Board of Education workshop item for the meeting of May 18, 2021. Twenty slides, authored around five guiding principles attributed to Cornelius Godfrey.

**Guiding Principles**
1. Radical Equity: dismantling systems of inequity takes courage, imagination and a high tolerance for discomfort.
2. Gracious Inclusion: invitations to "the table" extended not on the basis of perceived merit, but because it's time to eat.
3. Abundance Mentality: belief that available resources are sufficient to meet the needs of every child, everyday.
4. Fearless Feedback: an honest look at ourselves and actively seeking critique, without threat of reprisal.
5. Many Hands: the work can never be "my work," "your work" or "their work" — it must always be "our work."

**Where we've been**
The 2009 TSD Diversity Study, conducted by R&J Consulting Group (Rosalind Cox), produced findings and recommendations in four areas: Personnel Diversity (review hiring and recruiting practices with a focus on retention), Cultural Awareness (appoint a Diversity Council, establish staff-wide competencies and incorporate them into evaluation), Curriculum (review data for gaps in achievement and access; review materials for inclusivity), and Parent Outreach (establish parent networks). A Diversity Council convened meetings between 2011 and 2012.

**Where we are**

| Initiative | Participants |
| --- | --- |
| National Equity Project | District and building administrators, teachers, students |
| Teacher's College: TRWP | Teachers |
| Book Clubs | Elementary and secondary teachers, administrators, support staff |
| Excellence in Equity Statement | Board of Education |
| Leading for Equity | Teachers, support staff (early adopters) |
| Building-level training on Culturally Responsive Teaching | Dr. Jay Marks of Oakland Schools |
| Equity Survey by Hannover Research | All stakeholders (staff, students, parents) |

**Where we're going**
System-wide integration across all pillars, departments and content areas, with significant investment from Teaching & Learning; community voice through collaborative meetings and quantitative evidence; creation of a new Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion and Community Relationships role with three priorities; and an equity agenda calling for a comprehensive framework of supports at building and district levels (BELE), a learning continuum for all TSD employees, capacity building through stakeholder partnerships, transparency and reporting mechanisms, and a co-designed action plan with parent and student advisory support.

**Survey results**

| Respondent group | Count |
| --- | --- |
| Students (grades 5-12) | 5,520 |
| Parents | 1,503 |
| TSD staff members | 425 |
| Total stakeholder perceptions reflected | 7,448 |

Key finding: the greatest opportunity for improvement exists in the perceptions and experiences of Black students and Black parents. The final report was expected in late May or early June. Slides compare overall stakeholder perceptions against Black stakeholders, and overall parent perception against Black parents.

**Connecting**
Focused conversations with community members; Michigan Seal of Biliteracy; 70 scheduled connections via Calendly; an affinity group for TSD employees of color; postings shared to HBCUs via Handshake; MI Roundtable connections.

**Learning continuum**
A "house analogy" positions employees along three stages — Listening, Learning, Leading — described as a non-judgmental method of placing TSD employees along the continuum of learning for equity and inclusion.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document and occasion**

A Troy School District PowerPoint presentation of twenty slides titled "TSD Equity & Inclusion," prepared for an Equity and Inclusion Board Workshop held in connection with the Board of Education meeting of May 18, 2021. It narrates the district's equity history, current initiatives, survey results, planned structure, and a staff learning continuum.

**Guiding Principles**

Five numbered principles are presented, attributed on the slide to Cornelius Godfrey. Radical Equity holds that the work of dismantling systems of inequity takes courage, imagination and a high tolerance for discomfort. Gracious Inclusion states that invitations to "the table" are extended not on the basis of perceived merit, but because it is time to eat. Abundance Mentality asserts that to effectively engage in the work of equity one must believe available resources are sufficient to meet the needs of every child, everyday. Fearless Feedback holds that achieving equity requires an honest look at ourselves and actively seeking critique, without the threat of reprisal. Many Hands states that improving outcomes for the marginalized means the effort can never be "my work," "your work" or "their work" — it must always be "our work."

**Where we've been**

The historical anchor is the 2009 TSD Diversity Study conducted by R&J Consulting Group, with Rosalind Cox named as the consultant. A Diversity Council convened meetings between 2011 and 2012. The study's findings and recommendations are grouped into four areas. Personnel Diversity: review hiring and recruiting practices with a focus on retention. Cultural Awareness: appoint a Diversity Council, establish staff-wide competencies and incorporate them into the evaluation process. Curriculum: review data to identify gaps in achievement and access, and review materials for inclusivity. Parent Outreach: establish parent networks to review concerns and recommendations.

**Where we are**

Current initiatives are paired with the audiences engaged in each. The National Equity Project involves district and building administrators, teachers and students. Teacher's College TRWP involves teachers. Book Clubs involve elementary and secondary teachers, administrators and support staff. The Excellence in Equity Statement is attributed to the Board of Education. Leading for Equity involves teachers and support staff described as early adopters. Building-level training on Culturally Responsive Teaching is associated with Dr. Jay Marks of Oakland Schools. The Equity Survey by Hannover Research reaches all stakeholders — staff, students and parents.

**Where we're going and what's different now**

Five forward-looking themes are listed. System-wide integration means a place in all pillars, departments and content areas, with significant investment from Teaching & Learning. Community Voice covers collaborative meetings and quantitative evidence to support the work. The creation of a new equity role — Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion and Community Relationships — carries three priorities: Assess, Connect and Engage. The Equity Agenda calls for implementing a comprehensive framework of supports at the building and district levels, identified as BELE; establishing a learning continuum for all TSD employees; building capacity for equity leadership through stakeholder partnerships; transparency and reporting mechanisms; and a co-designed action plan with parent and student advisory support.

**Three Priorities in detail**

Assess: establish a baseline for current equity, inclusion and community relations; center the perspectives of marginalized stakeholders; gauge efficacy and implementation fidelity regularly. Connect: build dynamic stakeholder coalitions; empower stakeholders to advance equity and inclusion within their various spheres of influence; elevate the voices of marginalized students and families. Engage: focused action oriented toward positive outcomes for marginalized students and families; proactively respond to community concerns; enact practices aimed at systematizing equity and inclusion. Three source citations are footnoted: Bustamante, R. and J. Nelson, "The School-Wide Cultural Competence Checklist," 2007, at cnx.org; "Recommendations for Diversity Training," Arlington Public Schools, at apsva.us; and "Strategies for Promoting Culturally Responsive Classrooms," Alexandria City Public Schools, page 14, at acps.k12.va.us/equity/strategies.

**The Pulley Analogy**

A slide frames assessment, connections and engagement through a pulley. Assessment represents an accurate understanding of the size, weight and dimensions of the load. Connections are represented by the pulley itself, used to multiply and change the direction of effort. Engagement represents the work being done, aided by the mechanical and relational advantage of the pulley. A note adds that the work of advancing equity and inclusion must always be focused on improved outcomes for marginalized individuals and community members, and that efforts with no observable positive impact on the marginalized may be necessary as prerequisites for the work but are not themselves the work.

**Planned activities under each priority**

Under Assess: a comprehensive "Listening Tour" using qualitative methods (surveys, interviews, questionnaires, focus groups) and quantitative methods (a data deep dive for disparities in perceptions, discipline and academic outcomes), a community connections review, and a curriculum review. Under Connect: assemble a Community Advisory Board and a Student Advisory Board; develop a staff coalition district-wide and at building, subject-area and administration levels; establish feedback channels for staff and students; and partner with equity and inclusion exemplars at the district and ISD level. Under Engage: draft vision and mission statements; implement an accountability and transparency platform; develop a three-to-five-year strategic plan for equity and inclusion; develop research-based criteria for equity and inclusion; provide professional development; and establish norms for dialogue.

**Equity & Inclusion Survey results**

The assessment slide reports that the Equity & Inclusion Survey reflected 7,448 stakeholder perceptions, comprising 5,520 students in grades 5 through 12, 1,503 parents and 425 TSD staff members. The stated key finding is that the greatest opportunity for improvement exists in the perceptions and experiences of Black students and Black parents. The final report was expected in late May or early June. Two subsequent slides are given over to comparisons: overall stakeholder perceptions versus Black stakeholders, and overall parent perception versus Black parents.

**Connecting activity to date**

Reported connection work includes focused conversations with community members, the Michigan Seal of Biliteracy, 70 scheduled connections via Calendly, an affinity group for TSD employees of color, job postings shared to HBCUs via Handshake, and MI Roundtable connections.

**Equity & Inclusion Learning Continuum**

The final section presents a Troy School District learning continuum with three stages — Listening, Learning, Leading — introduced through a house analogy described as a non-judgmental method of positioning TSD employees along the continuum of learning for equity and inclusion. Listening involves examining practice for compliance with district equity and inclusion standards, establishing a working knowledge of key terms and definitions, and considering available on-ramps for additional learning. Learning involves reflection on practice to implement cultural competencies, taking responsibility for professional learning, identifying and confronting personal biases, and understanding the role of culture and identity in learning. Leading involves reflection on systems and practices, identifying equity challenges, analyzing data for disparities, and taking responsibility for the learning of others within one's sphere of influence.

**Continuum examples**

Listening examples include following district policy for course recommendation, completing an online training module on cultural competence, reviewing evaluation criteria with a direct supervisor, reading context-specific articles focused on equity, inclusion or diversity, and reviewing policies released by neighboring districts relating to equity and anti-racism. Learning examples include participating in a district-sponsored book study, viewing a documentary film and participating in a discussion group, attending trainings offered by TSD or other local organizations, designating an accountability partner to encourage engagement and learning, and engaging in county-level organizations with equity as a central focus. Leading examples include participating in the district's Leading for Equity learning series, developing systems of group reflection and accountability, leading discussion groups and book clubs to support learning and growth, identifying and addressing system-level barriers to equitable access and practice, and adopting policies that advance equitable and anti-racist practices.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Instrument and setting**
Resolution Authorizing 2021 Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation) (Taxable), Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, offered at a regular meeting of the Board of Education conducted electronically on March 16, 2021 at 7:00 p.m., prevailing Eastern Time. Mover, supporter, present/absent members, and AYES/NAYS are blank in the draft; the certification is signed by Gary Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education, citing the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976.

**Purpose**
Authority to refund comes from Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended (the Revised Municipal Finance Act). The Prior Bonds are the 2012 Refunding Bonds (General Obligation – Unlimited Tax), dated December 20, 2012, and the 2014 School Building and Site Bonds (General Obligation – Unlimited Tax), dated January 29, 2014. The Municipal Advisor advised that net present value savings of debt service costs may be achievable; the refunding is structured on a taxable basis.

**Authorized parameters**
| Item | Parameter |
| --- | --- |
| Maximum aggregate principal | $45,000,000 |
| Denomination | $5,000 or integral multiples |
| Maximum interest rate | 4.00% per annum |
| Interest payment dates | May 1 and November 1, semi-annually |
| Maturity | May 1 of years fixed at sale |
| Minimum net present value savings | 1.00% of projected debt service on the Refunded Bonds |
| Sale price range | not less than 99%, not more than 105% of par |

Final terms are delegated to the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually as an “Authorized Officer,” under Section 315(1)(d) of the Act.

**Funds and security**
Commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2020, the District must levy annually a tax sufficient to pay principal and interest, without limitation as to rate or amount, under Article IX, Sections 6 and 16 of the Michigan Constitution of 1963. A 2021 Refunding Bonds Debt Retirement Fund is opened unless a Common Debt Retirement Fund exists. Proceeds first fund a 2021 Refunding Bonds Costs of Issuance Fund, with any surplus moved to the Debt Retirement Fund; the balance goes to an Escrow Fund held by an Escrow Agent under an Escrow Agreement, invested in United States obligations to pay the Refunded Bonds.

**Sale mechanics**
Competitive public sale is the default, with a Notice of Sale published in the Bond Buyer, New York, New York, and award to the lowest true interest cost. Paragraph 11 permits a negotiated sale instead: a public offering through a selected senior Underwriter, or a private placement with a qualified bank or sophisticated institutional investor through a Placement Agent, in which case no continuing disclosure undertaking is required and the bonds may be exempt from the rating requirement of Section 323 of the Act.

Bond Counsel: Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone, P.L.C. Municipal Advisor: PFM Financial Advisors LLC, 555 Briarwood Circle, Suite 333, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48108, (734) 994-9700, facsimile (734) 994-9710.

**Recitals**
Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, the Revised Municipal Finance Act, permits refunding of funded indebtedness. The Prior Bonds are the 2012 Refunding Bonds (General Obligation – Unlimited Tax), dated December 20, 2012, and the 2014 School Building and Site Bonds (General Obligation – Unlimited Tax), dated January 29, 2014. The Municipal Advisor advised net present value savings of debt service costs may be accomplished. The Board determines it is in the District’s best interest to issue bonds not to exceed Forty-Five Million Dollars ($45,000,000) to advance refund all or a portion of the callable maturities of the Prior Bonds (the “Refunded Bonds”) on a taxable basis, and notes the District must be qualified or obtain prior approval from the Michigan Department of Treasury.

**Bond authorization and details (paragraphs 1–2)**
Bonds may be issued in one or more series, not exceeding $45,000,000 or such lesser amount as determined by the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually (each an “Authorized Officer”). Bonds are registered as to principal and interest in the denomination of $5,000 or integral multiples, dated as of delivery, numbered by the Transfer Agent, maturing May 1 in years and amounts set at sale. Interest may not exceed four percent (4.00%) per annum, payable semi-annually on May 1 and November 1, provided net present value savings are not less than one percent (1.00%) of projected debt service on the Refunded Bonds absent the refunding, based on Treasury guidelines. Sale price must be not less than 99% and not more than 105% of principal. Serial or term bonds are permitted; term bonds designated by the original purchaser carry mandatory redemption per the Notice of Sale schedule. Interest is paid by check mailed to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month prior to the payment date. Book-entry-only issuance through The Depository Trust Company, New York, New York, is permitted.

**Execution, tax levy, funds, proceeds (paragraphs 3–6)**
Bonds follow Exhibit A, signed by manual or facsimile signatures of the President and Secretary of the Board, valid only upon Transfer Agent authentication, delivered per instructions from the Treasurer of the School District. Commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2020, the District must levy annually a tax sufficient to pay principal and interest when due, without limitation as to rate or amount, as permitted by Article IX, Section 6 and Article IX, Section 16 of the Michigan Constitution of 1963. Unless a Common Debt Retirement Fund exists, the Treasurer opens a 2021 Refunding Bonds Debt Retirement Fund; tax proceeds, accrued interest on delivery, and any net original issue premium are deposited there, and premium may reduce the principal amount issued if federal tax law requires. Proceeds fund a 2021 Refunding Bonds Costs of Issuance Fund, with any surplus transferred to the Debt Retirement Fund; the balance, plus money transferred from the debt retirement fund for the Refunded Bonds, is invested in direct obligations of or obligations unconditionally guaranteed by the United States of America in one or more Escrow Funds held by a bank or trust company as trustee and Escrow Agent under Escrow Agreements irrevocably directing redemption of the specified Prior Bonds.

**Sale, ratings, disclosure, negotiated alternatives (paragraphs 7–12)**
The Authorized Officer may fix a sale date, publish notice in the Bond Buyer, New York, New York, in the form of Exhibit B, award to the bidder producing the lowest true interest cost, and execute a sale order without further Board direction. Bond ratings and municipal bond insurance may be pursued if deemed appropriate by the Municipal Advisor and Bond Counsel. The District covenants under SEC Rule 15c2-12 to provide the Exhibit C information. A negotiated sale is permitted: a public offering with a selected senior Underwriter and optional co-managing underwriters, or a private placement with a qualified bank or sophisticated institutional investor (the “Purchaser”) via a Placement Agent, with an Exhibit D certificate, no continuing disclosure undertaking, possible exemption from the rating requirement of Section 323 of the Act, and a private placement memorandum in lieu of the Official Statement. Final details may be adjusted under Section 315(1)(d) of the Act.

**Professionals, Treasury, further actions (paragraphs 13–17)**
Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone, P.L.C. is appointed Bond Counsel; PFM Financial Advisors LLC is appointed Municipal Advisor. Treasury waivers, including rating waivers, and a Security Report are authorized, as is qualification under the School Bond Qualification, Approval, and Loan Act, Act 92, Public Acts of Michigan, 2005, as amended, with the Secretary directed to submit the Application for Final Qualification in the form of Exhibit E. Payable costs of issuance include Bond Counsel fees, Municipal Advisor fees, rating agency fees, Transfer Agent fees, Escrow Agent fees, and official statement printing. Conflicting resolutions are rescinded.

Interest is computed on a 360-day year of twelve 30-day months, first payable in 2021 and semiannually thereafter, maturing May 1. The bond recites Act 451, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, as amended, Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, and the resolution adopted March 16, 2021; pledges full faith, credit and resources; states bonds are not subject to optional redemption prior to maturity; requires sixty (60) days’ mailed notice of a Transfer Agent change; and sets the record date at the fifteenth (15th) day of the month.

Definitions include Audited Financial Statements required by Act 2, Public Acts of Michigan, 1968, as amended; EMMA, the MSRB’s Electronic Municipal Market Access system; Financial Obligation; and the Rule, SEC Rule 15c2-12 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A summary sheet prepared for the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) bylaws review lists each proposed 2025 revision by page, article and section with a short rationale. Four revisions are identified as clerical or grammatical and are stated not to change the meaning of the bylaws, including correcting 'off' to 'office' in Article V, Section 3 and 'Ther' to 'The' in Article VIII, Section 2. Eight further sections are revised for content, among them a new Article VII, Section 10 requiring the Board of Directors to create and maintain Board Operating Procedures, an option to split the Office of Secretary into Corresponding and Recording Secretary roles, and a shift of committee-chair elections from the first meeting after January 31st to the first meeting after July 1st. Article XVI, Section 1 would let the Board of Directors correct grammatical errors without a vote of the membership, while substantive amendments still go to Member School Districts on a written ballot with at least a forty (40) day voting period.

Overview
OCSBA Bylaws - Amendments at a Glance is a change-log style handout accompanying the Oakland County School Boards Association's proposed 2025 bylaws revisions. Each entry gives the page number, article, section, the revised language and a rationale. The revisions are divided into two groups: four clerical/grammatical changes stated not to change the meaning of the bylaws, and eight sections revised and edited for content.

Clerical and grammatical revisions
| # | Page | Article / Section | Change and rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 3 | Article V, Sec. 3 - Place of Meeting | 'off' is supposed to read 'office' (registered office of the Association) |
| 2 | 6 | Article VIII, Sec. 2 - Term of Office | Delete the stray 'r' so 'Ther' reads 'The' |
| 3 | 9 | Article IX, Sec. 4 - Government Relations Committee | Add 'on' after 'information' |

| # | Page | Article / Section | Substance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 5 | Article VII, Sec. 4 - Notice | Delete references to notice by U.S. mail and fax as outdated modes of communication; special-meeting notice given at least two days by written notice delivered personally, by phone or email |
| 2 | 6 | Article VII, Sec. 10 - Board Operating Procedures | New section: the Board shall create and maintain Board Operating Procedures to be used with the Bylaws, reflecting procedures recently adopted that define roles, responsibilities and timelines |

| 5 | 9 | Article IX, Sec. 4 - Government Relations Committee | Standing committee meeting at least 6 times per year; each Member School District appoints a representative at its annual organizational meeting; chair elected annually at the first committee meeting after January 31st with one (1) vote per district; in the absence of an elected Vice Chair the Vice President of OCSBA assumes the position |
