https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: American Cancer Society consumer health article titled “Cell Phone Towers,” last medically reviewed and last revised June 1, 2020, included in the June 15, 2021 board packet as agenda item 9.D. It states that at this time there is no strong evidence that exposure to radiofrequency (RF) waves from cell phone towers causes any noticeable health effects, while cautioning that this does not mean the waves are proven absolutely safe. Ground-level RF energy near typical cellular base stations is described as hundreds to thousands of times less than the safe-exposure limits set by the US Federal Communication Commission, and the ACS itself takes no official position on whether RF radiation causes cancer.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Source and status**
Article “Cell Phone Towers” from the American Cancer Society, cancer.org, 1.800.227.2345, written by the American Cancer Society medical and editorial content team. Last Medical Review: June 1, 2020. Last Revised: June 1, 2020. Eleven pages including hyperlinks, additional resources and a reference list. Provided in the June 15, 2021 Troy School District board packet as agenda item 9.D.

**Core conclusion**
At this time there is no strong evidence that exposure to RF waves from cell phone towers causes any noticeable health effects; this does not mean the waves have been proven absolutely safe, and most expert organizations agree more research is needed, especially on possible long-term effects.

**How towers expose people**
Base stations can be free-standing towers or mounted on existing structures such as trees, water tanks or tall buildings, and are usually from 50 to 200 feet high. RF waves sit in the electromagnetic spectrum between FM radio waves and microwaves and are non-ionizing, so they do not directly damage DNA, unlike x-rays, gamma rays and ultraviolet rays. Antenna energy is directed toward the horizon with some downward scatter. At ground level near typical cellular base stations, RF energy is hundreds to thousands of times less than the US Federal Communication Commission (FCC) limits for safe exposure. Roof exposure can exceed ground levels only very close to and directly in front of antennas. Indoors, energy behind an antenna is hundreds to thousands of times lower than in front, and wood or cement block reduces exposure by a factor of about 10.

**What expert agencies say**
The American Cancer Society has no official position or statement on whether RF radiation from cell phones, towers or other sources causes cancer, and looks to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), part of the World Health Organization, and the US National Toxicology Program (NTP), formed from parts of the National Institutes of Health, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and Food and Drug Administration. Neither IARC nor NTP has classified the cancer-causing potential of RF waves from cell phone towers specifically. The FCC is quoted stating that emissions from cellular and PCS antennas produce ground-level exposures typically thousands of times below safety limits and that there is no reason to believe such towers could constitute a potential health hazard to nearby residents or students. Based on studies published up until 2011, IARC classified RF radiation as “possibly carcinogenic to humans.” The FDA, reviewing studies published between 2008 and 2018, concluded there is insufficient evidence to support a causal association between radiofrequency radiation exposure and tumor formation. The NTP has not included RF radiation in its Report on Carcinogens.

**Studies cited**
A large British study of families of young children with cancer found no link between a mother's exposure to towers during pregnancy and early childhood cancer risk. Researchers in Taiwan found slightly higher overall cancer risk in children living in towns with estimated RF exposure above the study midpoint, a finding less apparent under other exposure categorizations; both studies relied on estimated rather than measured exposure. Large 2018 studies by the NTP and the Ramazzini Institute in Italy found increased risk of malignant schwannomas, uncommon heart tumors, in male rats but not female rats or mice, with the NTP also reporting possible increased risks of brain and adrenal gland tumors; a 2019 review by the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) found the studies' limitations did not allow conclusions about RF energy causing cancer.

**5G**
Earlier generation networks used wavelengths below 6 gigahertz (GHz); 5G uses some of that range plus higher frequencies at the lower end of the millimeter wave spectrum, which ranges from 30 GHz to 300 GHz. These remain non-ionizing. Higher frequency waves travel shorter distances and penetrate objects less well, so 5G requires many more small cells mounted on streetlights, utility poles and buildings, typically at much lower power than macro base stations. Very little research has shown that 5G RF waves are any more or less of a concern than other cellular RF wavelengths.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The American Cancer Society article “Cell Phone Towers,” carrying the cancer.org and 1.800.227.2345 banner, was included in the Troy School District Board of Education packet for June 15, 2021 as agenda item 9.D. Its stated dates are Last Medical Review: June 1, 2020 and Last Revised: June 1, 2020, and it is written by the American Cancer Society medical and editorial content team, described as doctors and oncology certified nurses along with journalists, editors and translators. The material is copyrighted, with reprint requests governed by the ACS Content Usage Policy.

Overview. The article opens by noting that widespread cell phone use in recent decades has led to a large increase in the number of cell phone towers, also known as base stations, placed in communities, and that these towers have electronic equipment and antennas that receive and transmit cell phone signals using radiofrequency (RF) waves. Its central conclusion is that at this time there is no strong evidence that exposure to RF waves from cell phone towers causes any noticeable health effects, but that this does not mean the RF waves have been proven absolutely safe, and most expert organizations agree more research is needed, especially regarding possible long-term effects.

How towers expose people to RF waves. Cell phone base stations can be free-standing towers or mounted on existing structures such as trees, water tanks or tall buildings; antennas must be high enough to cover a given area, and base stations are usually from 50 to 200 feet high. Cell phones communicate with nearby towers mainly through RF waves, a form of energy in the electromagnetic spectrum between FM radio waves and microwaves. Like FM radio waves, microwaves, visible light and heat, RF waves are non-ionizing radiation and do not directly damage the DNA inside cells, which is how stronger ionizing radiation such as x-rays, gamma rays and ultraviolet (UV) rays is thought to cause cancer. An electromagnetic spectrum illustration credited to the National Cancer Institute shows frequencies from extremely low (such as power lines) to extremely high (such as x-rays and gamma rays). At very high levels RF waves can heat body tissues, but the levels used by cell phones and towers are much lower. When a call is placed, a signal goes from the phone's antenna to the nearest base station antenna, the base station assigns an available RF channel, RF waves transfer voice information to the base station, and voice signals are sent to a switching center that transfers the call to its destination, with signals relayed back and forth during the call; the RF waves produced at the base station are given off into the environment where people can be exposed.

Exposure by location. On the ground near a tower, RF waves from the antenna are directed toward the horizon, parallel to the ground, with some downward scatter. Base station antennas use higher power levels than other land-mobile antennas but much lower levels than radio and television broadcast stations, and RF energy decreases rapidly as distance from the antenna increases, so ground-level exposure is much lower than exposure close to the antenna. At ground level near typical cellular base stations, the amount of energy from RF waves is hundreds to thousands of times less than the limits for safe exposure set by the US Federal Communication Commission (FCC) and other regulatory authorities, and it is very unlikely a person could be exposed above these limits merely by being near a tower. On a roof with a cellular antenna, a person could be exposed to levels greater than those on the ground, but levels approaching or exceeding FCC safety guidelines are only likely very close to and directly in front of antennas, and access to such areas should be limited. Indoors with a base station mounted on the outside of a building, RF energy is typically much lower than outside, depending on construction materials; antennas point away from the building side, energy behind the antenna is hundreds to thousands of times lower than in front, and wood or cement block reduces exposure by a factor of about 10, so exposure in a room directly behind the wall is typically well below recommended exposure limits.

What expert agencies say. The American Cancer Society (ACS) does not have any official position or statement on whether RF radiation from cell phones, cell phone towers or other sources causes cancer, and generally looks to other expert organizations to determine whether something is a carcinogen, including the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), part of the World Health Organization (WHO), and the US National Toxicology Program (NTP), formed from parts of several government agencies including the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). So far neither IARC nor the NTP has classified the cancer-causing potential of RF waves from cell phone towers specifically. The article quotes the FCC on towers near homes or schools: radiofrequency emissions from antennas used for cellular and PCS (personal communications service) transmissions result in exposure levels on the ground that are typically thousands of times below safety limits, limits adopted by the FCC based on recommendations of expert organizations and endorsed by federal agencies responsible for health and safety, so there is no reason to believe such towers could constitute a potential health hazard to nearby residents or students.

On RF radiation generally, IARC, based on a review of studies published up until 2011, classified RF radiation as “possibly carcinogenic to humans,” citing limited evidence of a possible increase in risk for brain tumors among cell phone users and inadequate evidence for other cancer types. More recently the US FDA issued a technical report based on studies published between 2008 and 2018 as well as national cancer rate trends, concluding there is insufficient evidence to support a causal association between radiofrequency radiation (RFR) exposure and tumor formation. The NTP has not included RF radiation in its Report on Carcinogens, which lists exposures known to be or reasonably anticipated to be human carcinogens.

Studies described. Researchers generally use studies looking at groups of people and studies done in the lab using lab animals or cell cultures. Few studies in people have focused specifically on cellular phone towers and cancer risk, and results have not provided clear answers. A large British study comparing families of young children with cancer to families of children without cancer found no link between a mother's exposure to towers during pregnancy, based on distance from home to the nearest tower and on RF energy given off by nearby towers, and the risk of early childhood cancer. Researchers in Taiwan comparing children with cancer to similar children without cancer found slightly higher overall cancer risk among those living in towns with estimated RF exposure from towers above the study's midpoint level, though the finding was less apparent when exposure was categorized in other ways. Both studies relied on estimated rather than measured RF exposure. Exposure from living near a tower is typically many times lower than exposure from using a cell phone; several dozen studies have examined links between cell phone use and tumors, and most have not found a link, with important limitations noted.

Lab studies. RF waves from towers do not have enough energy to damage DNA directly or heat body tissues, so it is not clear how towers might cause cancer. Large studies published in 2018 by the US National Toxicology Program and by the Ramazzini Institute in Italy exposed groups of lab rats, and mice in the NTP study, to whole-body RF waves for many hours a day beginning before birth and continuing for most or all of their natural lives. Both found an increased risk of uncommon heart tumors called malignant schwannomas in male rats but not in female rats, nor in male or female mice in the NTP study; the NTP study also reported possible increased risks of certain brain and adrenal gland tumors. A 2019 review of the two studies by the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) determined that their limitations did not allow conclusions about the ability of RF energy to cause cancer, though the results do not rule out the possibility of health impacts.

5G networks. Fifth generation cellular networks are being rolled out in the United States and other countries and can transmit much larger amounts of data over shorter periods than 4G, 3G and earlier generations. Earlier generations used RF wavelengths below 6 gigahertz (GHz); 5G uses some wavelengths in that range plus higher frequencies at the lower end of the millimeter wave spectrum, which ranges from 30 GHz to 300 GHz. These higher-frequency waves remain non-ionizing and still lack the ability to directly damage DNA. Because they travel shorter distances and pass less well through objects such as buildings or tree leaves, 5G requires many more small cells, which can be mounted on streetlights, utility poles, buildings and other structures, placing antennas closer to people while typically operating at much lower power than larger macro base stations. Adding higher wavelengths could expose people to more RF waves overall, though higher frequency waves penetrate the body less and in theory might be less likely to have health effects; this has not been well studied, and there has been very little research showing 5G RF waves are any more or less of a concern than other cellular RF wavelengths.

Resources and references. Additional resources listed include the FCC RF Safety FAQ, the FDA Cell Phones page, the National Cancer Institute fact sheets on Cell Phones and Cancer Risk and Electromagnetic Fields and Cancer, and National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences pages on Electric and Magnetic Fields and Cell Phone Radio Frequency Radiation, with a note that inclusion does not imply ACS endorsement. Cited references include ANSI-C95.1, 1982, American National Standards Institute, safety levels for human exposure to radiofrequency electromagnetic fields, 300 kHz to 100 GHz; Elliott P, Toledano MB, Bennett J, et al., Mobile phone base stations and early childhood cancers: Case-control study, BMJ 2010;340:c3077; Falcioni L, Bua L, Tibaldi E, et al., report on brain and heart tumors in Sprague-Dawley rats exposed from prenatal life until natural death to a mobile phone radiofrequency field representative of a 1.8GHz GSM base station environmental emission, Environ Res 2018;165:496-503; FCC Office of Engineering and Technology RF Safety FAQ, 2015, accessed December 30, 2019; FDA, Review of Published Literature between 2008 and 2018 of Relevance to Radiofrequency Radiation and Cancer, 2020, accessed March 19, 2020; IEEE-C95.1, 1991, safety levels for human exposure to radio frequency electromagnetic fields, 3 kHz to 300 GHz, Piscataway, NJ; IEEE, Human exposure to RF emissions from cellular radio base station antennas, Washington, DC, 1992; IARC Monographs Volume 102: Non-ionizing Radiation, Part 2: Radiofrequency Electromagnetic Fields, 2013, accessed December 4, 2019; ICNIRP, Health issues related to the use of hand-held radiotelephones and base transmitters, Health Phys 1996;70:587-593; ICNIRP Note critically evaluating the two 2018 animal carcinogenicity studies, Health Phys 2019 Aug 27; IRPA, 1988, International Radiation Protection Association guidelines on limits of exposure to radio frequency electromagnetic fields; Li CY, Liu CC, Chang YH, Chou LP, Ko MC, A population-based case-control study of radiofrequency exposure in relation to childhood neoplasm, Sci Total Environ 2012 Oct 1;435-436:472-478; National Council on Radiation Protection (NCRP) 1986 Report 86, Biological effects and exposure criteria for radiofrequency electromagnetic fields, Bethesda, MD, pp. 1-382; NIEHS Cell Phone Radio Frequency Radiation Studies, 2019, accessed December 27, 2019; Repacholi M, van Deventer E, Ravazzani P, eds., Base stations and wireless networks: Exposures and health consequences, World Health Organization, accessed December 30, 2019; and Röösli M, Frei P, Mohler E, Hug K, Systematic review on the health effects of exposure to radiofrequency electromagnetic fields from mobile phone base stations, Bull World Health Organ 2010 Dec 1;88(12):887-896F.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: "Radiofrequency and Public Health" is a four-page white paper by David M. Hamby, Ph.D., dated November 2006 and carried as item 9.D. in the June 15, 2021 Troy Board of Education packet. Hamby, a professor of health physics at Oregon State University and a former University of Michigan School of Public Health professor, measures typical PCS and cellular tower output against federal exposure guidelines. Its central figure is that the maximum power density 100 feet laterally from a cell antenna element calculates to 0.010 mw/cm2, or 100 times below the NCRP limit of 1 mw/cm2, and it concludes that health risks from PCS or cellular RF transmissions are negligible.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Document and author**
White paper titled "Radiofrequency and Public Health / The Impact of Radiofrequency Transmissions on Public Health," by David M. Hamby, Ph.D., November 2006; four numbered pages. Hamby is Professor of Health Physics (radiation protection) at Oregon State University, a former professor in the University of Michigan's School of Public Health and a graduate of the University of North Carolina's School of Public Health, with 20 years in environmental and occupational health protection including 6 years as a research scientist with Westinghouse. He serves on Scientific Committee #64-23 of the NCRP and Committee N13.60 of ANSI, sits on the editorial boards of Health Physics and Environmental Monitoring and Assessment, and has served as a technical expert for the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

**Scope and units**
Public concern that began with extremely low frequency fields near electric-power lines has extended to radiofrequency transmissions used in wireless communications; the paper surveys typical exposure levels and federal guidelines in the PCS and cellular range. Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz), one repetition per second; a heart beating 70 times per second beats at 70 Hz, and a 1 GHz chip performs 1 billion operations per second. PCS operates in the 1.9 GHz range. Power is measured in Watts; a 100 W bulb uses twice the energy of a 50 W bulb, and PCS towers output about 200 Watts in each of three sectors. Exposure limits are expressed as power density in mw/cm2, where 1000 milliwatts equals 1 Watt.

**Exposure limits**

| Body / jurisdiction | Public limit |
| --- | --- |
| FCC (standardization suggested August 1, 1996, adopting NCRP recommendation) | 1 mw/cm2 |
| Australia and New Zealand | identical to NCRP |
| Netherlands | twice that value |
| ICNIRP (2 GHz and higher) | 1 mw/cm2 |

Limits are set into law by the FCC on recommendation from the IEEE, ANSI and NCRP. For perspective, the metabolic heat production rate of an average human at rest is about 5 mw/cm2, rising with activity to as much as 80 mw/cm2 depending on age, gender, size and physical fitness.

**Calculated tower emissions**

| Distance from antenna | Maximum power density | Relation to standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 100 feet | 0.010 mw/cm2 | 100 times lower |
| 200 feet | 0.0025 mw/cm2 | 400 times lower |
| 400 feet | 0.00063 mw/cm2 | 1,600 times lower |

Power density equals total power divided by the area through which it is directed; for a typical cell tower that area is 4πr2/6, the surface of a spherical triangle of radius r with a horizontal angle of 120 degrees and a vertical angle of approximately 90 degrees. The worked example uses a transmitter output of 200 Watts (200,000 milliwatts) and a distance of 100 feet (3,048 centimeters). Because the inverse-square principle applies, doubling the distance reduces power density four times. Actual ground-level values are lower still because most transmitted power is aimed at the horizon.

**Comparison with other RF sources**
A table lists anti-theft devices, automatic door openers, hand-held cellular, cordless phones, CB radio, mobile radio, PCS, microwave ovens, satellite communications, AM radio, FM radio, LORAN transmitters and television by frequency range (MHz) and maximum power (Watts). Television and radio towers are generally much taller and emit up to 5 million Watts; a 1,000 foot TV tower radiating 5 million Watts in all directions would have a power density at its base of 0.43 mw/cm2, more than 40% of the federal limit at that frequency. Baby monitors operate at a few Watts, so the power density 100 feet from a 200 Watt PCS transmitter equals that about four feet from a baby monitor.

**Conclusion**
Calculated and measured PCS power densities are many times lower than the 1 mw/cm2 standard. Most recent studies find no statistical difference between exposed and non-exposed persons; the minority reporting associations generally cannot establish causation, and rat studies frequently fail to replicate, one group's own triplicate experiment yielding one positive and two negative findings. Scientific studies have failed to demonstrate a human health effect from low-level radiofrequency fields, and risks from PCS or cellular RF transmissions are called negligible.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
"RADIOFREQUENCY AND PUBLIC HEALTH: The Impact of Radiofrequency Transmissions on Public Health" is a four-page white paper written by David M. Hamby, Ph.D., dated November 2006, distributed as agenda item 9.D. for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of June 15, 2021.

**Author credentials.** Dr. Hamby is described as currently Professor of Health Physics (radiation protection) at Oregon State University and a former professor in the University of Michigan's School of Public Health. He is a graduate of the University of North Carolina's School of Public Health and has spent 20 years studying environmental and occupational health protection, including 6 years working as a research scientist with Westinghouse. He serves on Scientific Committee #64-23 of the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (NCRP) and on Committee N13.60 of the American National Standards Institute (ANSI). He sits on the Editorial Board for the Health Physics journal and for the journal of Environmental Monitoring and Assessment, and has served as a technical expert for the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

**Framing of the issue.** Over the past several years, the paper states, potential health impacts from exposure to electromagnetic fields have gained widespread public interest. Questions arose originally with regard to extremely low frequency electric and magnetic fields such as those found near electric-power lines. With the continued advancement of personal communications technology, similar concerns have arisen about electromagnetic transmissions in the radiofrequency region, including that used in wireless communications. The paper provides an overview of typical exposure levels and current federal exposure guidelines for radiofrequency electromagnetic waves in the frequency range utilized by PCS and cellular systems.

**Frequency and power.** Biological effects associated with exposure to intense electromagnetic fields, generally the result of thermal heating, depend on two characteristics of electromagnetic waves: frequency and power. Using speech as an analogy, frequency corresponds to pitch (treble or bass) and power to loudness. The scientific unit of frequency is the Hertz (Hz), representing one repetition per second; a heart beating 70 times per second would beat at a frequency of 70 Hz, and a computer chip operating at 1 GHz (gigahertz, giga meaning billion) performs 1 billion operations per second. A figure in the paper, an electromagnetic spectrum chart labeled with frequency in MHz and wavelength in meters, shows common uses across the spectrum — AM, FM, TV, mobile radio, CB radio, cordless phones, PCS, microwaves, infrared, visible light and x-rays — with a boundary marked between non-ionizing and ionizing radiation. PCS operates in the 1.9 GHz frequency range.

Power is measured in Watts (W), the amount of energy transferred during one second; a 100 W light bulb uses twice the energy of a 50 W light bulb. PCS towers operate at a typical power output in each of three sectors of about 200 Watts.

**Regulatory limits.** Radiofrequency exposure limits for members of the general public are set into law by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) based on recommendations from the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) and the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (NCRP). Today's standards identify the amount of energy per second, usually in milliwatts (1000 milliwatts equals 1 Watt), that can be transmitted through a square inch or, more typically, a square centimeter. Limits are therefore expressed as "power density" in mw/cm2 (milliwatts per square centimeter). On August 1, 1996 the FCC suggested standardization of exposure limits and adopted the NCRP recommendation of 1 mw/cm2. Regulations enacted within the previous couple of years in Australia and New Zealand stipulate identical limits to those of the NCRP, and regulations in the Netherlands allow exposure limits twice this value. The International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) has also adopted an exposure limit of 1 mw/cm2 for members of the general public at frequencies of 2 GHz and higher.

**Metabolic comparison.** These limits are placed in perspective by comparison with the metabolic heat production rate for an average human at rest, about 5 mw/cm2. With increased activity, the metabolic heat production rate can naturally rise to as much as 80 mw/cm2, depending on physiological parameters such as age, gender, size and general physical fitness. The paper states that the heat production rate in the body caused by metabolism is thousands of times greater than any heat generated as a result of these transmissions.

**Calculated tower exposure.** PCS and cellular systems emit electromagnetic waves at frequencies in the GHz range with a nominal power of about 200 Watts per sector. Under these conditions the maximum power density at 100 feet laterally from the antenna element is calculated to be 0.010 mw/cm2, or 100 times below the NCRP limit. That estimate assumes transmission power is emitted equally in all directions within the focused area. In practice the bulk of transmitted power is aimed only at the horizon, so actual power levels on the ground 100 feet from the base of the tower are much less than the calculated value. Such power densities are far below the federal limit and a great deal lower than levels at which any type of biological effect has been observed.

**Comparison with other RF sources.** To illustrate what these power densities mean, the paper compares PCS transmissions with power density levels of other well-known radiofrequency devices, including baby monitors, anti-theft monitors and automatic door openers at department stores, cordless telephones, police/fire two-way radios, and television and radio broadcasting stations. Standard television and radio towers are generally much taller than PCS or cellular towers and emit signals with power levels up to 5 million Watts. A 1,000 foot TV tower holding an antenna that emits 5 million Watts in all directions potentially has a power density at its base of 0.43 mw/cm2, more than 40% of the federal limit for emissions at that frequency. Baby monitor transmitters operate at a power of a few Watts; therefore the power density at a distance of 100 feet from a 200 Watt PCS transmitter would equal the power density at about four (4) feet from a baby monitor. An accompanying table, "Some common radiofrequency sources," lists by frequency range (MHz) and maximum power (Watts) the following sources: anti-theft device, automatic door opener, hand-held cellular, cordless phone, CB radio, mobile radio, PCS, microwave oven, satellite communications, AM radio, FM radio, LORAN transmitter and television.

**Review of the literature.** The paper summarizes that calculated and measured power densities resulting from PCS transmissions are many times lower than the national and international RF standard of 1 mw/cm2. The most recent literature on potential health effects of RF exposure continues to show that a vast majority of studies find no statistical difference between exposed and non-exposed persons for the various biological effects studied. A few investigators suggest their data show associations between exposure and biological effect, but these studies are generally unable to establish a causal relationship. Repeated studies of effects on rats are many times unable to reproduce results; one group of investigators conducting their experiment in triplicate showed one positive and two negative findings for a particular biological effect in rats following exposure to radiofrequency radiation, a result the paper cites as demonstrating the variability of such research. Scientific studies have failed to demonstrate a human health effect from exposure to low-level radiofrequency electromagnetic fields, and the scientific data indicate that health risks from PCS or cellular RF transmissions are negligible.

**Calculation of maximum power density.** Power density can be calculated at any distance from an electromagnetic source if the source is assumed to emit from a single point: the total power emitted divided by the area through which the power is directed. For a typical cell tower that area is 4πr2/6, the surface area of a spherical triangle with radius r, a horizontal angle of 120 degrees and a vertical angle of approximately 90 degrees. The worked example assumes a transmitter power output of 200 Watts (200,000 milliwatts) and the shortest distance associated with an urban tower, 100 feet (3,048 centimeters). Because the inverse-square principle applies to electromagnetic emission sources, every doubling of distance reduces power density four times: at 100 feet horizontally from the top of a cell tower the maximum power density is 0.010 mw/cm2 (100 times lower than the RF standard); at 200 feet it would be four times lower, about 0.0025 mw/cm2 (400 times lower than the standard); and at 400 feet it is reduced to 0.00063 mw/cm2 (1,600 times lower than the standard). Power density therefore drops very rapidly with increasing distance from the emission source.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: "RF Measurements Help to Win Lease Approval" is a site-leasing feature from the May 2009 issue of AGL (Above Ground Level) magazine, included as item 9.D. in the June 15, 2021 Troy Board of Education packet. It recounts a January 5 vote by the Marshalltown (Iowa) Community School District Board of Education to keep in place an agreement with U.S. Cellular for a tower resembling a light pole at the Marshalltown High School football field. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Publication**
Site-leasing article, "RF Measurements Help to Win Lease Approval," AGL (Above Ground Level) magazine, May 2009, pages 16, 18 and 19, www.agl-mag.com.

**The decision**
Members of the Marshalltown (Iowa) Community School District Board of Education voted in the majority to keep in place a previously approved agreement with U.S. Cellular for a proposed cell tower that would take the place of, yet resemble, a light pole at the Marshalltown High School football field. The vote was taken on January 5 and followed concerns brought to the board by residents near the school about possible health effects of radio-frequency emanations from the tower. Although the Telecommunications Act of 1996 does not allow government agencies to take health effects of RF emitted from cell towers and other radio transmitters into account when making site-approval decisions, landlords may consider health effects when deciding whether to lease.

**The presenter**
U.S. Cellular asked Marv Wessel of Global RF Solutions, Chandler, Ariz., to speak to board members about possible health effects. Wessel later described his presentation to AGL.

**The BioInitiative Report**
Local activists promoted a website against the proposed site, and one or more board members and residents referenced the "BioInitiative Report: A Rationale for a Biologically-based Public Exposure Standard for Electromagnetic Fields (ELF and RF)," published at www.bioinitiative.org. Wessel said the report claims a diverse range of adverse health effects related to RF emissions while dismissing the Nationwide Cohort Study in Denmark by Christoffer Johansen, John D. Boice Jr., Joseph K. McLaughlin and Jorgen H. Olsen, which included 420,095 cell phone users and found no significant link between cell phone use and cancer. The report suggests reducing RF exposure limits without specifying values, other than that "a precautionary limit of 0.1 µW/cm2 (which is also 0.614 volts per meter) should be adopted for outdoor, cumulative RF exposure." Wessel noted that any properly designed cellular or PCS site, with antennas at least 10 meters above ground level, already contributes less than that proposed precautionary limit in surrounding areas, while commercial TV and FM broadcast levels typically exceed it in every major metropolitan location in the country.

**Measurement method**
Wessel presented quantitative RF measurements taken with a selective radiation meter — a spectrum analyzer plus an isotropic antenna, the Narda SRM-3000 — one of a few portable spectrum analyzers designed and calibrated specifically for RF compliance safety measurements. It has a dynamic range much greater than broadband equipment and can discriminate measurements by frequency from 50 to 3000 MHz, isolating each license holder's contribution to the overall RF environment. With narrowband selectivity, power density levels can be measured down to the picowatt per square centimeter level.

**The handset argument**

| Condition | RF exposure to students |
| --- | --- |
| Serving cell site a mile or two away | handsets at full power; peak level 1,000 times below FCC limit |
| Cell site nearby | handsets at significantly lower power; level 1 million times below the safety limit |

At the Marshalltown school, service came from sites a mile or two away, and Wessel's measurements indicated handsets were powered up to full power during a call because the distant cell site controls handset power based on the received uplink signal. He told the board a quarter-watt handset next to the head delivers significantly more energy to the user than a 100-watt cell site 100 feet away and 100 feet above the ground, because of the inverse-square law, under which RF energy at a distance from a source drops by the square of the distance.

**Other points**
Wessel described measurements in a New York City neighborhood where FM and TV broadcast signals contributed a greater percentage of overall RF energy than a cell site across the street, with the total still well below the safety limit. He said objections are sometimes based on hysteria, that a worker on a tower may come close enough to an antenna — especially FM or TV broadcast antennas — to require an RF suit, and that a person would have to scale a cactus-disguised tower to its hidden antennas to receive unsafe exposure. A majority of the board members were persuaded, though "some people are never satisfied."
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
"RF Measurements Help to Win Lease Approval" is a site-leasing feature published in the May 2009 issue of AGL (Above Ground Level) magazine (pages 16, 18 and 19; www.agl-mag.com), reproduced as agenda item 9.D. for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of June 15, 2021. Its subhead states that showing how placing a cell site near a high school would reduce RF emissions from wireless handsets used by students helped persuade a board of education to leave in effect a previously approved lease for a tower at an athletic field.

**The Marshalltown decision.** Members of the Marshalltown (Iowa) Community School District Board of Education voted in the majority to keep in place an agreement with U.S. Cellular for a proposed cell tower that would take the place of, yet resemble, a light pole at the Marshalltown High School football field. The vote was taken on January 5. It came about as a result of concerns brought to the board by residents near the school regarding the possible effect upon health that radio-frequency emanations from the tower might have. The article notes that although the Telecommunications Act of 1996 does not allow government agencies to take into account the health effects of RF emitted from cell towers and other radio transmitters when making decisions about site approval, landlords may consider health effects when deciding whether to lease. A photo caption observes that cell towers near schools sometimes raise questions about possible health risks.

**The consultant.** U.S. Cellular asked Marv Wessel of Global RF Solutions, Chandler, Ariz., to speak to the board members about possible health effects. Afterward, AGL asked Wessel about his presentation, and the article is built around his account.

**Opposition and the BioInitiative Report.** Wessel said that in addition to local activists promoting a website against the proposed site, one or more board members and residents made reference to the "BioInitiative Report: A Rationale for a Biologically-based Public Exposure Standard for Electromagnetic Fields (ELF and RF)," published on the web at www.bioinitiative.org. "The report claims there is a diverse range of adverse health effects related to RF emissions," Wessel said. He stated that the BioInitiative Report seems to completely dismiss the Nationwide Cohort Study in Denmark by Christoffer Johansen, John D. Boice Jr., Joseph K. McLaughlin and Jorgen H. Olsen, which included 420,095 cell phone users and found no significant link between cell phone use and cancer.

Wessel called it peculiar that the BioInitiative Report suggests RF exposure limits be reduced to increase the safety margin against the possibility of nonthermal effects on humans without offering specifics on what those limits should be, beyond the suggestion that "a precautionary limit of 0.1 µW/cm2 (which is also 0.614 volts per meter) should be adopted for outdoor, cumulative RF exposure." The irony, Wessel explained, is that any properly designed cellular and PCS site, which would have antennas at least 10 meters above ground level, already contributes less than what the BioInitiative Report proposes as a precautionary limit to areas surrounding those sites. He pointed out that commercial TV and FM broadcast levels typically exceed this precautionary limit in every major metropolitan location in the country: "Curiously, they choose to ignore an RF source that has been present for several decades."

**"Better science."** Wessel said that although the BioInitiative Report appears to have as its objective making the case for eliminating or reducing wireless communications, in several places the report admits there is no definitive link between cell phones and cancer. In preparing his presentation, Wessel viewed a website built by one of those opposed to the tower: "He had the BioInitiative Report on his site along with other information depicting a one-sided view against cell towers."

**Measurement equipment.** Wessel presented the board a different perspective based on quantitative RF measurements taken with a selective radiation meter, which consists of a spectrum analyzer and an isotropic antenna — the Narda SRM-3000. He said this meter is one of a few portable spectrum analyzers designed and calibrated specifically to make safety measurements for RF compliance and to provide evidence that energy levels may be many times less than the safety minimum. "It has a dynamic range much greater than broadband equipment specifically designed to perform RF compliance measurements," he said, adding that "you can discriminate these measurements by frequency from 50 to 3000 MHz. This enables us to specifically measure each license holder's contribution to the overall RF environment."

**The handset exposure argument.** Wessel described the RF measurement data that was persuasive for the Marshalltown board. "They were concerned about the RF level that would be present at the high school if they allowed the cell site to be built. Actually, the larger risk of RF exposure comes from the cellular handset itself, even though it's still greatly below the FCC limits." He cited the inverse-square law, which says that the RF energy at a distance from a source drops by the square of the distance from the source.

At the Marshalltown school, cellular service is provided by sites a mile or two away, which causes the handsets used at the school to emit their highest RF power output, because the distant cell site controls handset power and raises or lowers it according to the received signal (uplink) at the cell site. "I took measurements at the school, and they indicated the handsets were powered up to full power during a call because of the distance to the serving cell site," Wessel said. "I told the board that it could reduce the RF exposure to students using phones by putting a site nearby because then the handsets would operate at significantly lower power. If you have a quarter-watt handset next to your head, it delivers significantly more energy to the user than does a 100-watt cell site 100 feet away and 100 feet above the ground, because of the inverse-square law."

"But no one ever looks at it that way," Wessel said. "They see the cell site as an RF radiation problem next to the school. But ironically, when you put the cell site next to a high school, where kids are huge users of handsets, the handset's power is significantly reduced by thousands of times. A nearby site actually helps the issue." One parent observed that students have handsets near their heads all the time. "Our measurements proved that with a nearby cell site, RF exposure from the handsets would be reduced from a level 1,000 times (peak) below the FCC-defined safety limit to a level 1 million times below the safety limit," Wessel said. "A majority of the board members were persuaded by this approach. But some people are never satisfied."

**Actual measurements and public reaction.** Wessel said the fact is that handsets are going to be powered down if the cell site is nearby, and the RF exposure from the handset is the greater risk. Despite the evidence, some people do not want to look at the actual measurements, and their objection is sometimes based on hysteria. "The cell sites look ominous, but the power reaching the ground in the vicinity of the site is insignificant," he said. He also described measurements he made in a New York City neighborhood where RF energy reaching the neighborhood from FM and TV broadcast signals is a greater percentage of the overall RF energy than the portion delivered by a cell site across the street. "They don't want to hear that, either," he said of residents opposing a neighborhood cell site. "They fear the long-term effects of RF exposure from cell sites, yet FM and TV signals have been on the air for a lot longer than cellular signals, they represent a higher percentage of the overall RF exposure than the cellular signals do, and the total is still well below the safety limit."

**Common-sense approach and narrowband selectivity.** Wessel said the idea is to present information in a common-sense approach. "You're never going to change the opinion of a skeptic or of the conspiracy theorists who want to believe that the explosion in cell site growth will cause significant health risks," he said. "They call it new technology, but it's merely a new application of old technology. You can rarely change their minds. You try to present a common-sense approach to people who have become emotional by the surrounding hysteria. The cellular site opponents get people worked up and cite possible children's health effects in an effort to convince them that the cellular sites are harming the kids." With measurement equipment capable of narrowband selectivity, Wessel said, it is possible to select a frequency and measure power density levels down to the picowatt per square centimeter level: "It allows you to demonstrate that cell sites are not a big deal."

**Illustrations.** Photographs show Wessel using a selective radiation meter to take measurements and taking RF measurements near a cellular antenna disguised as a saguaro cactus; the captions note that a person would have to scale the cactus to the antennas hidden near its top to receive unsafe RF exposure, and that although a worker on a tower may come close enough to an antenna — especially FM or TV broadcast antennas — to require protection in the form of an RF suit, the inverse-square law shows the intensity of RF from an antenna rapidly diminishes as distance increases, so that away from the tower energy levels rarely surpass the health limit, especially for cellular antennas.

**Membership Structure (MASB Bylaws, Article IV, Section 2)**
The board of education of any public school district in Michigan may become an active member. Active members are divided into eight regions designated by intermediate school district boundaries. Region 1 covers Copper Country ISD, Delta-Schoolcraft ISD, Dickinson-Iron ISD, Eastern Upper Peninsula ISD, Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD, Marquette-Alger RESA and Menominee County ISD. Region 8 covers Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools and Wayne RESA. Members are also divided into seven groups by pupil membership: Group I all intermediate districts; Group II 0-1,400; Group III 1,401-2,500; Group IV 2,501-5,000; Group V 5,001-11,000; Group VI 11,001-40,000; Group VII more than 40,000.

**Board Composition and Limits**
The MASB Board of Directors comprises 24 members, including three at-large directors. Sixteen directors are elected from the eight regions, two per region, and one director per group is elected from Groups V, VI and VII. The MASB President nominates at-large directors subject to Board approval. Article VIII, Section 6 permits only one director from any one local or intermediate school district board. Article VIII, Section 8 provides that an unopposed nominee is declared elected without an election.

**Seats Up in 2024**
Nine seats, one each, three-year terms unless noted: Regions 1 (open seat), 2, 3 (one-year term), 4 (one-year term), 5, 6 (open seat), 7, 8, and Group V (one-year term).

| Seat | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Region 1 | Vacant; no nominations received |
| Region 2 | Dawn Kaiser, Iosco RESA, unopposed |
| Region 3 | Rick Dernberger, Zeeland Public Schools and Ottawa Area ISD, unopposed |
| Region 4 | John Tramontana, DeWitt Public Schools, unopposed |

**Voting Procedure**
Each district received one ballot, emailed to the superintendent secretary on record with MASB on Jan. 26, 2024; ballots cannot be forwarded. Completed ballots must be cast and confirmed by the superintendent secretary by 1 p.m. on Wednesday, March 6, 2024. Unofficial results are posted to the voicemail recording at 517.327.5915, generally after 2 p.m. on the deadline date, and emailed that afternoon; official results are approved at the March 22, 2024 Board of Directors' meeting. No local district or ISD funds may be used to campaign, including use of district email accounts; questions go to MASB Legal Counsel Brad Banasik, J.D., bbanasik@masb.org, 517.327.5929. The Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) 2024 Board of Directors elections booklet, presenting the bylaws framework for membership, the schedule and rules for the 2024 election, and biographical and statement pages for each candidate.

**Membership regions.** Under MASB Bylaws Article IV, Section 2, the board of education of any public school district in Michigan may become an active member. Active members are divided into eight regions designated according to intermediate school district boundaries. Region 1: Copper Country ISD, Delta-Schoolcraft ISD, Dickinson-Iron ISD, Eastern Upper Peninsula ISD, Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD, Marquette-Alger RESA and Menominee County ISD. Region 2: Alpena-Montmorency-Alcona ESD, Charlevoix-Emmet ISD, Cheboygan-Otsego-Presque Isle ESD, COOR ISD, Iosco RESA, Manistee ISD, Northwest Education Services and Wexford-Missaukee ISD. Region 3: Ionia County ISD, Kent ISD, Mecosta-Osceola ISD, Montcalm Area ISD, Muskegon Area ISD, Newaygo County RESA, Ottawa Area ISD and West Shore ESD. Region 4: Bay-Arenac ISD, Clare-Gladwin RESD, Clinton County RESA, Gratiot-Isabella RESD, Midland County ESA, Saginaw ISD and Shiawassee RESD. Region 5: Genesee ISD, Huron ISD, Lapeer County ISD, Sanilac ISD, St. Clair County RESA and Tuscola ISD. Region 6: Allegan Area ESA, Barry ISD, Berrien RESA, Branch ISD, Calhoun ISD, Heritage Southwest ISD, Kalamazoo RESA, St. Joseph County ISD and Van Buren ISD. Region 7: Eaton RESA, Hillsdale County ISD, Ingham ISD, Jackson County ISD, Lenawee ISD, Livingston ESA, Monroe County ISD and Washtenaw ISD. Region 8: Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools and Wayne RESA.

**Membership groups.** Active members are also divided into seven groups based on pupil membership: Group I, all intermediate districts; Group II, school districts with a pupil membership of 0-1,400; Group III, 1,401-2,500; Group IV, 2,501-5,000; Group V, 5,001-11,000; Group VI, 11,001-40,000; and Group VII, more than 40,000.

**Board composition and election rules.** Nine seats on the MASB Board of Directors were up for election in 2024. The Board comprises 24 members, including three at-large directors. Sixteen directors are elected from the eight regions, two from each region, and one director per group is elected from Groups V, VI and VII. The MASB President nominates a member to serve as an at-large director, subject to Board approval. Article VIII, Section 6 of the MASB Bylaws permits only one director to be elected or appointed from any one local or intermediate school district board. Article VIII, Section 8 provides that if any nomination is unopposed, the Board of Directors declares the unopposed candidate elected without conducting an election for that group or region.

**Seats and uncontested outcomes.** The seats up were Regions 1 (open seat), 2, 3 (one-year term), 4 (one-year term), 5, 6 (open seat), 7, 8 and Group V (one-year term), one seat each and three-year terms unless otherwise noted. Region 1 had a vacant seat as no nominations were received. Region 2 continues to be represented by Dawn Kaiser, Iosco RESA (unopposed, no ballots sent). Region 3 continues with Rick Dernberger, Zeeland Public Schools and Ottawa Area Intermediate School District (unopposed). Region 4 continues with John Tramontana, DeWitt Public Schools (unopposed). Group V continues with Stephen Hyer, Clarkston Community Schools (unopposed). Voting in Regions 5, 6, 7 and 8 took place via online ballot.

**Voting procedures.** Each district received one ballot, emailed to the superintendent secretary on record with MASB on Jan. 26, 2024; ballots could not be forwarded. Boards conveyed their choice to the superintendent secretary, and completed ballots had to be cast and confirmed by 1 p.m. on Wednesday, March 6, 2024. Unofficial results were made available on the voicemail recording at 517.327.5915, generally after 2 p.m. on the deadline date, and emailed that afternoon; official results were to be approved at the March 22, 2024 Board of Directors' meeting, which newly elected directors should plan to attend. No local district or ISD funds could be used to campaign, a rule that prohibits candidates from using school district email accounts to message other board members, requiring a personal account instead; questions about what constitutes an expenditure of district funds go to MASB Legal Counsel Brad Banasik, J.D., at bbanasik@masb.org or 517.327.5929. An electronic file of physical and email addresses for the voting group or region was made available to each candidate under a revocable license limited to contacting school board members about the election. General questions were directed to Cheryl Huffman at 517.327.5915 or chuffman@masb.org.

**Region 5 candidates.** Janice Holz, incumbent, Huron Intermediate School District, Huron County: 32 years on that board and 25 years on the Bad Axe Public Schools board, having held President, Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer on both; MASB certifications include Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember Award, Master Diamond Award, Master Platinum Award, President's Award of Recognition, Advocacy Specialty and Data Specialty. Her motto is that passion and positivity can make the impossible happen; contact 810.936.1615, roshawnda.williams63@gmail.com.

A former classroom teacher, central office administrator for operations and school superintendent, he volunteers on the boards of Court Appointed Special Advocates, Barry County Community Mental Health Authority, Barry Intermediate School District and the Family Support Center of Barry County, and has served on the MASB Government Relations Committee. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Summary sheet prepared by the Oakland County School Boards Association listing the proposed 2025 amendments to its bylaws, organized as four clerical or grammatical corrections that do not change meaning followed by eight sections revised for content, each keyed to page, article and section with a rationale. The most substantive changes add a new Article VII, Section 10 requiring the Board of Directors to create and maintain Board Operating Procedures, allow the Office of Secretary to be split into Corresponding and Recording Secretary roles, and move committee chair elections from after January 31st to after July 1st to align with the July 1 - June 30 operating year.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Purpose**
An "Amendments at a Glance" companion to the redlined OCSBA bylaws, identifying each proposed change by page, article and section and giving the committee's rationale. The changes are split into two groups: clerical/grammatical revisions that do not change meaning, and sections revised and edited for content.

**Clerical and grammatical revisions (four)**
1. Page 3, Article V, Section 3, Place of Meeting - correcting "off" to "office" where the text refers to the registered office of the Association as the default meeting place.
2. Page 6, Article VIII, Section 2, Term of Office - deleting the stray "r" so "Ther" reads "The" in the section governing officer terms, removal with cause by affirmative vote of a majority of the Directors, and the filling of vacancies.
3. Page 9, Article IX, Section 4, The Government Relations Committee - adding "on" after "information" in the description of the standing committee, which meets at least 6 times per year.
4. Page 15, Article XIV, Section 2, Dealing with the Association - removing a duplicated phrase in the conflict-of-interest provision on contracts between the Association and its directors or officers.

**Revisions for content (eight)**
1. Page 5, Article VII, Section 4, Notice - deleting language on giving special meeting notice by fax and by U.S. mail, described as outdated modes of communication; notice of a special meeting of the Board of Directors is given at least two days by written notice delivered personally, by phone, fax, or email.
2. Page 6, Article VII, Section 10, Board Operating Procedures - new section requiring the Board of Directors to create and maintain Board Operating Procedures to be used in conjunction with the bylaws, added because the Board recently adopted such procedures defining roles, responsibilities and timelines.
3. Page 7, Article VIII, Section 6, The Secretary - permitting the Board, at its discretion on an annual basis, to divide the Office of Secretary into Corresponding Secretary and Recording Secretary; rationale cites a Board of 7-9 directors and additional leadership opportunities.
4. Page 8, Article IX, Section 3, Committee Chairs - moving the chair election from the first committee meeting after January 31st to after July 1st, with written notice of the election date, time and place at least seven (7) calendar days before the vote; rationale is alignment with the July 1 - June 30 operating year.
5. Page 9, Article IX, Section 4, The Government Relations Committee - membership and leadership language providing that each Member School District appoint a representative at its annual organizational meeting, that each district in attendance has one (1) vote cast by its appointed representative, and that in the absence of an elected Vice Chair the Vice President of OCSBA assumes the position, to build leadership on GRC.
6. Page 9, Article IX, Section 5, Resolutions and Bylaws Committee - shifting appointment of committee members from the Board of Directors to the OCSBA President annually, consistent with common practice; the Government Relations Committee Chairperson is a member of the committee, which meets at least once per year.
7. Page 16, Article XV, Section 5, Method of Giving Notices - replacing mailing with electronic communication to a director's or officer's last known district-provided email address, because OCSBA does not physically mail communications.
8. Page 17, Article XVI, Section 1, Amendments - retaining amendment by vote of the Member School Districts on a written ballot with at least a forty (40) day voting period and one vote per district, while allowing the Board of Directors to correct grammatical errors that do not change meaning or intent without a vote of the membership.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
"OCSBA Bylaws - Amendments at a Glance" is the crosswalk document accompanying the redlined Oakland County School Boards Association bylaws presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on May 20, 2025. It sorts the proposed 2025 amendments into two categories and gives, for each, the page number in the bylaws, the article and section affected, the operative language, and a rationale.

CLERICAL AND GRAMMATICAL REVISIONS
The document states that four revisions are clerical or grammatical in nature and do not change the meaning of the bylaws.

First, Page 3, Article V, Section 3, Place of Meeting. The Board of Directors may designate the place of meeting for any annual or regular meeting or for any special meeting; if no designation is made, or if a special meeting is otherwise called, the place of the meeting will be the registered office of the Association; but if all of the Members meet at any time and place and consent to holding of a meeting, such meeting will be valid without call or notice, and at such meeting any corporate action may be taken. Rationale: grammar and clarification, since "off" is supposed to be "office."

Second, Page 6, Article VIII, Section 2, Term of Office. The term of office for all officers commences upon their election or appointment and continues until the next annual meeting of the Association and thereafter until their respective successors are chosen or until their resignation or removal. Any officer may be removed from office at any meeting of the Directors, with cause, by the affirmative vote of a majority of the Directors, whenever in their judgment the best interests of the Association will be served thereby. An officer may resign by written notice to the Association, effective upon receipt or at a subsequent time specified in the notice. The Directors have power to fill any vacancies in any offices occurring for whatever reason. Rationale: grammar/clarity - deleting the "r" in the first word to change "Ther" to "The."

Third, Page 9, Article IX, Section 4, The Government Relations Committee. The Government Relations Committee shall be a standing committee whose purpose is to receive information on legislative matters for the purpose of sharing said information with the Member School Districts to advocate for, and increase awareness of, issues facing public education. The committee will meet at least 6 times per year. The correction inserts "on" after "information."

Fourth, Page 15, Article XIV, Section 2, Dealing with the Association. The provision states that a contract or other transaction between the Association and one or more of its directors or officers, or between the Association and a domestic or foreign corporation, firm or association of any type or kind in which one or more of the Association's directors or officers are trustees or officers, or are otherwise interested, is not void or voidable solely because of such common trusteeship, officership or interest, or solely because such directors are present at the meeting of the Board of Directors or committee thereof at which such contract or transaction is acted upon, or solely because their votes are counted for such purpose, if any of the stated conditions is satisfied. Rationale: to remove a duplicate phrase.

SECTIONS REVISED AND EDITED FOR CONTENT
The document then lists eight sections revised for content.

1. Page 5, Article VII, Section 4, Notice. Notice of any special meeting of the Board of Directors will be given at least two days by written notice delivered personally, by phone, fax, or email to each Director's contact information as shown by the records of the Association, or five days' notice by mail; if mailed, such notice is deemed delivered when deposited in the United States mail in a sealed envelope so addressed with postage prepaid. Any Director may waive notice; attendance at any meeting constitutes waiver except where a Director attends for the express purpose of objecting to the transaction of business because the meeting is not lawfully called or convened. Neither the business to be transacted at, nor the purpose of, any regular or special meeting need be specified in the notice or waiver unless specifically required by law or the bylaws. Rationale: deleting language that refers to sending meeting notices via U.S. mail and fax, which are outdated modes of communication.

2. Page 6, Article VII, Section 10, Board Operating Procedures. A new section reading: "The Board of Directors shall create and maintain Board Operating Procedures which shall be used in conjunction with these Bylaws." Rationale: adding this section as the Board of Directors recently adopted Board Operating Procedures that further define roles, responsibilities and timelines.

3. Page 7, Article VIII, Section 6, The Secretary. The Secretary attends all meetings of the Board of Directors and records all votes and the minutes of all proceedings in a book kept for that purpose; gives or causes to be given notice of all meetings of the Directors for which notice may be required; performs other duties as prescribed by the Directors; and has authority to execute with the President all authorized conveyances, contracts or other obligations in the name of the Association, except as otherwise directed by the Directors. The amendment adds that at the discretion of the Board of Directors on an annual basis, the Office of Secretary may be divided into two roles: Corresponding Secretary and Recording Secretary. Rationale: with a Board of 7-9 directors, it is helpful to split the role of Secretary into two and provides additional leadership opportunities.

4. Page 8, Article IX, Section 3, Committee Chairs. Each standing and ad hoc committee shall elect a Chairperson annually from the appointed representatives, with the election as the first order of business at the committee's first meeting after July 1st, replacing January 31st, unless otherwise specified in the bylaws. Written notice of the election date, time and place shall be provided to all appointed representatives not less than seven (7) calendar days prior to the meeting at which the vote will occur. Rationale: the Operating Year is July 1 - June 30 and this change brings the bylaws into alignment.

5. Page 9, Article IX, Section 4, The Government Relations Committee. Beyond the standing committee description and the at-least-6-meetings-per-year requirement, the amendment adds Committee Membership/Leadership language: at each Member School District's annual organizational meeting, a Member should be appointed to represent that district on the Government Relations Committee; a Committee Chairperson will be elected annually from the appointed Members at the first committee meeting after January 31st; each Member School District in attendance shall have one (1) vote, cast by the district's appointed representative; and in the absence of an elected Vice Chair, the Vice President of OCSBA will assume the position of Vice Chair. Rationale: to ensure the association is building leadership on GRC.

6. Page 9, Article IX, Section 5, Resolutions and Bylaws Committee. The committee is a standing committee that develops and manages the resolutions and bylaws process and meets at least once per year. Under Committee Membership/Leadership, committee members will be appointed by the OCSBA President annually rather than by the Board of Directors; members may be reappointed for additional terms; the appointed members elect a Committee Chairperson at the first committee meeting after appointment; and the Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member of the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee. Rationale: common practice is that the OCSBA President makes committee appointments.

7. Page 16, Article XV, Section 5, Method of Giving Notices. Any notice required by statute or by the bylaws to be given to the directors, or to any officers of the Association unless otherwise provided, shall be given by electronic communication to such director or officer at his or her last known district-provided email address as the same appears on the records of the Association, and such notice shall be deemed to have been given at the time of such communication - replacing the prior references to mailing. Rationale: OCSBA does not physically mail communications.

8. Page 17, Article XVI, Section 1, Amendments. The bylaws may be altered or amended by the vote of the Member School Districts; the Board of Directors will provide a written ballot with the proposed amendment(s) to each Member School District giving at least a forty (40) day period in which to vote, and each Member School District will have one vote. The amendment adds that grammatical errors that do not change the meaning or intent of the language may be corrected by the Board of Directors without a vote of the membership. Rationale: small grammatical errors such as grammar and spelling that do not change meaning or intent can be corrected by the Board of Directors during the annual review rather than having to go out to the membership for a vote.

Taken together, the package modernizes notice provisions from mail and fax to email, codifies Board Operating Procedures in the bylaws, creates flexibility to split the Secretary role, realigns committee chair elections and appointment authority with the association's July-to-June operating year and the President's customary appointment power, and gives the Board limited authority to fix typographical errors without a full membership ballot.

The document carries adoption history of Board of Directors 11/15/2017, General Membership 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018, and amendments approved by Member School Districts on 9/16/2020, 9/10/2021 and 3/3/2023, and runs from Article I offices at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, through Article XVI amendments plus Appendix 1 defining cause for removal.

**Identification and adoption history**
Bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association, shown with tracked changes and rationale notes. Adopted by Board of Directors 11/15/2017; adopted by General Membership 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018; amendments approved by Member School Districts 9/16/2020, 9/10/2021 and 3/3/2023.

**Articles I-V: offices, purpose, membership, dues, member meetings**
The principal office is at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland, Michigan. Purposes include advancing public education quality in Oakland County, sponsoring programs in partnership with Oakland Schools, and advocating for legislation supporting public education. Membership is open to publicly elected board members of Oakland County school districts and elected Oakland ISD board members whose districts are in good standing with MASB. Each Member has one vote; each Member School District has one vote on resolutions and bylaw amendments. Electronic voting is granted to the Board of Directors only for emergency business. Financing comes from an annual MASB grant to CASBA members, ISD dues not exceeding the MASB CASBA grant, and contributions. There is an annual meeting plus not less than three additional regular membership meetings; the annual meeting is the first regular meeting after July 1; special meetings require 30 days' notice; written notice of meetings is delivered not less than ten nor more than fifty days before; a quorum is at least one Member from twenty-five (25%) percent of Member School Districts.

**Articles VI-VIII: directors and officers**
The Board consists of an odd number of Directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9, with three-year terms and only one Member per district serving at a time. By May 1st yearly an Election Committee of the three most recently elected Directors is convened; elections occur at the June meeting; nominations cannot be made from the floor. Failure to attend three (3) consecutive Board meetings constitutes a resignation absent an excused absence requested in writing within thirty (30) days. Special meeting notice is at least two days; a majority is a quorum. New Section 10 requires Board Operating Procedures. Officers are President, Vice-President, Secretary and Treasurer; the Secretary role may be divided into Corresponding and Recording Secretary at the Board's annual discretion.

**Article IX: committees**
Quorum is twenty-five (25%) percent of appointed representatives. Chairs are elected at the first meeting after July 1st (changed from January 31st) with seven (7) calendar days' written notice. The Government Relations Committee meets at least 6 times per year; the OCSBA Vice President serves as Vice Chair absent an elected one. The Resolutions and Bylaws Committee meets at least once per year, with members appointed by the OCSBA President. Member School District voting windows are at least forty (40) calendar days, and resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) Member School Districts become the official position of the Association.

**Articles X-XVI and Appendix 1**
Dissolution follows Article VIII of the Articles of Incorporation; no inurement under Section 501(c)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Board approval and signature of both President and Treasurer are required for any expenditure exceeding $2,500; expenditures up to $2,500 need either the President or Treasurer. The Treasurer presents a budget for the fiscal year (July 1 to June 30) no later than the June Board meeting and end-of-year revenue and expense reports no later than August 30th. The Board may enter an Administrative and Financial Services Agreement with Oakland Schools. Article XII provides indemnification under the Michigan Nonprofit Association Act. Notices are given by electronic communication to district-provided email addresses. Appendix 1, adopted by the OCSBA Board of Directors on September 16, 2020, defines cause for removal by reference to the duties of care, loyalty and obedience.
